text: Laboratory note. Series 14. Seawater, the Ardmore approaches. Drawn 9th November 1866. Occasion of the work is entered as follows. The brig Cordelia Vane, 190 tons, was lost in the approaches on the night of the 2nd in thick weather. Whether she struck or foundered is not determined. No survivor speaks to the moment. Her cargo was not discharged and is taken to remain aboard her. The position is poorly taken. No cross bearings were obtained. The reckoning had run since the previous noon and the reported latitude is not relied upon. The ground to be searched is therefore broad. Four bottles drawn at the flood, four at the slack, on a line across the approaches. Depth, hour and state of tide entered against each. Bottles stoppered, sealed and numbered. Analysis deferred until the position is better fixed. Note filed with the tracing.

SURVEY REPORT, made at Stranraer this 12th day of November, 1861, upon the brig CORDELIA VANE, of 190 tons register. The vessel was lost in the approaches to Loch Ryan on the night of the 4th instant, the weather being thick with rain and the land not seen. Whether she struck upon a hard bottom or foundered from strain I am unable to determine, no part of her being visible at low water. Her cargo remained wholly on board at the time of loss, nothing having been landed or thrown overboard. The position is poorly taken. The master's reckoning and the mate's differ by upwards of two miles; no cross bearing was obtained, and the lead was hove but twice. I recommend that a further search be made in settled weather, the ground being soft brackish sediment. JAMES CROMBIE, Surveyor.

Assessment on the brig Cordelia Vane, 190 tons register, lost in the approaches to the Tarbert narrows. Weather thick two days before, with rain and no sight of sun or land. The last position given is by reckoning only, with no bearing to any mark. I do not trust it within five miles. Whether she struck the ground and filled, or foundered of herself in the sea then running, is not proved and cannot be. No man of her saw the bottom. Her cargo was aboard and remained aboard. Nothing landed, nothing lightened, no salvage rendered, no part of her come ashore but a boat's thwart and a hatch cover. Hull, total loss. Cargo, total loss. No unseaworthiness proved against her owners. The reported position is too coarse to found a search upon. Recommend payment in full. J. Amory, assessor, 1866.

The Marchioness of Ayr was lost in the approaches to Machrihanish bay on the night of the 14th November, 1869, in thick weather. She was outward bound with her cargo still aboard, none of it discharged and none since recovered. Fog had lain over the approaches from the forenoon, and no bearing had been obtained for some hours before she struck. Whether the vessel struck upon the ground and afterwards foundered, or foundered outright, is not determined; the surviving hands differ upon the point. The position handed in was taken by reckoning alone, no observation being possible, and is held by this Board to be poorly taken and not to be relied upon. The vessel has not been found.

BOOK OF THE WORKS. Account 41. Marchioness of Ayr, iron steamer, 1420 tons register. 1877. Account closed, the ship being lost. Word came down from Kilbrannan Sound that she was gone in the approaches, in thick weather, with her cargo still in her holds and nothing discharged. Whether she struck or foundered of herself is not established, and no man of her people will say which. The position handed in by the boats is a coarse one, got by guess in the fog without sight of land or star, and the two accounts of it differ by better than three miles. Castings, bearing brasses, and spare gear supplied to this vessel and unpaid: carried to Bad Debts by resolution of the partners. Charge upon the works, 214 pounds 6 shillings. No salvage reported. No further order to be entered against this name.

Assessment of loss. Steamer Marchioness of Ayr, iron built, 1,420 tons register. I have taken the master's statement and the mate's, and set down what I find. She was in the approaches on the night of the 3rd in thick weather, fog on her from the forenoon, no sight had of the land nor of any light. She struck, as the master believes, on the Gantock shoal, though the mate will say only that she took the ground or else opened a plate; the accounts do not agree and I cannot settle them. She filled and went down within the hour. Her whole cargo was aboard her, no part landed, no part thrown over. The position returned to me is by the master's reckoning alone. He had run some hours by log and lead with the tide against him, and I hold the spot doubtful by two miles or better. I recommend the loss be admitted as total, and that nothing be allowed for salvage until the wreck is found, which on such a position may be long.

Foundry Ledger, folio 214. Year 1871. Account: Marchioness of Ayr, iron steamer, 1,420 tons register. Goods consigned per the above and not delivered: Bearings, brass, 4 cwt 2 qr 14 lb. Bushes, 11 off, gross 318 lb. Cocks and unions, 96 lb. Total shipped, 12 cwt 0 qr 4 lb, charged at 1s. 4d. the pound. Remarks. The vessel was lost in thick weather in the approaches, Loch Ryan, the whole of the above cargo still aboard her and no part of it landed. Whether she struck or foundered is not returned to us. Her position was poorly taken: two bearings have been sent in and they differ by upwards of two miles, and no sounding was got at the place. Underwriters decline until the position is fixed. Recovery judged doubtful, concretion being reported on such fittings as have been raised thereabouts. Carried to suspense account: 89l. 6s. 2d.

ASSESSMENT No. 219. 1866. Vessel: Marchioness of Ayr. Iron steamer. 1420 tons register. Loss: total. Weather at the material hour: thick, fog on the water, no observation obtainable. Cause: not determined. Two of her people speak of a shock felt forward; the mate holds she filled and foundered of herself. Both accounts admitted, neither preferred. Cargo: aboard at the time of loss. Not discharged. Not recovered. Manifest annexed. Place: stated as the approaches at the Tarbert narrows. Position doubtful. Reported by dead reckoning only. No bearing taken, no lead recorded. Assessor notes the reported place cannot be relied upon nearer than several miles. Search: two boats, three days. Nothing found. Recommendation: total loss admitted; cargo interest likewise. Salvage prospects nil while the place of the wreck remains unfixed. Signed for the office.

Sir, - In reply to yours of the 3rd instant, and touching the steamer Marchioness of Ayr, iron built, of 1,420 tons, I set down what I know, whereof I had the account from two of her people at Kilbrannan Sound. FIRST, that the said vessel was lost in thick weather in the approaches, no observation having been obtained on that day nor on the day preceding. SECONDLY, that she struck, or else foundered of her own leak, the survivors being divided upon the point and neither version capable of proof. THIRDLY, that her cargo remained wholly aboard her at the time of loss, none of it having been landed, lightened, or jettisoned. FOURTHLY, that the position entered in the report was taken by reckoning only, and is in my judgment not to be relied upon, the tide having set her some distance she did not allow for. I am, sir, unable to say more with certainty, and I would not have you build upon that position. Yours faithfully.

Machrihanish, the 3rd of March 1876. Sir, You ask what I know of the Marchioness of Ayr and I will set it down plain, for I have no more than this. She was lost in thick weather in the approaches. I was not aboard her. I have it from two who were. One says she struck; the other says she opened and foundered under them. I cannot settle it and I will not pretend to. Her cargo was still aboard her when she went. Nothing was landed out of her. Nothing came ashore in this bay but staves and one hatch cover. Her position was poorly taken. They had no sight of the sun for a day and better, and the mate marked her down by guess. I have dragged twice on the bearing he gave and found clean sand and no iron at all. She lies somewhere off this bay in salt water and that is all any man can tell you. Yours truly, J. Crawfurd.

Survey made this day upon the reported wreck of the Marchioness of Ayr, iron steamer of 1420 tons, lost in the approaches to Sanda roads in thick weather in the winter of 1869. The vessel was on passage inward when she was overtaken by fog and lost the land. She either struck upon a shoal and settled after, or foundered without striking; the accounts of the crew do not agree, and there is not evidence enough to say which. Her cargo was not discharged before the loss and lies in her still, no part of the lading having been lifted or salved. The position entered at the time of the loss was got by dead reckoning, no sight of sun or land having been had for upwards of a day, and it is a poor position. Search was made upon it in 1870, and again this summer, and nothing was found. The wreck is not fixed.

Assessment of the claim arising upon the loss of the iron steamer Marchioness of Ayr, 1420 tons, the said vessel having been lost in the Ardmore approaches in thick weather. The underwriters do not dispute that the loss was occasioned by perils of the sea. It is not established, and in the opinion of the assessors cannot now be established, whether she struck upon the ground and thereafter foundered, or foundered without having struck, the weather being thick at the time and no observation of the land obtainable. The cargo was aboard at the moment of the loss, no part thereof having been discharged, and no part thereof having since been recovered or salved; the claim upon the cargo is accordingly allowed in full. As to the place of the loss, the assessors find the position returned to have been taken by reckoning only, and to be so poorly taken that no salvage of the vessel can be undertaken upon it.

HARBOUR MASTER'S LOG, Sanda roads. Wednesday, 14th June 1876. Wind SW, force 3, falling to 2 by evening; barometer 30.02 inches and steady; visibility good; no swell of consequence. 8h 40m a.m. The iron steamer Marchioness of Ayr, 1,420 tons register, reported off the north point, steaming by her own log 8 knots. Came to anchor in 6 fathoms, sand and shell, veering 30 fathoms of chain, at 9h 12m. Master reports the passage down from the Clyde in 11 hours 20 minutes, nothing whatever to note; engines worked throughout without stoppage; coal expended 19 tons. Landing of cargo commenced 10h, completed 4h 15m p.m.: 240 tons general merchandise, 80 tons cut peat in bales, 14 casks. Tallies taken by my assistant at the crane agreed with the ship's manifest to within two packages, which were afterwards found on the quay and duly entered. No damage reported, no complaint entered, no injury to any person. Dues paid at the office. Weighed 6h p.m., proceeding south. I enter the whole as routine in every particular. I note only, for the record and not as a matter arising out of this vessel, that the inner leg has shoaled by about one foot since the sounding of April, which I attribute to the run of the spring tides rather than to any true alteration of the bank.

Harbour master's log, 1876. April 11th. Marchioness of Ayr, iron steamer, 1420 tons, in from the westward off the Skerryvore ground, moored at the north buoy at six in the evening. Dues levied at the tonnage rate, 3 pounds 11s 4d, paid the same night by her mate, in coin, which I note because it is rare enough to be worth noting. Mooring: north buoy until the 14th, then shifted to the inner berth at my order to let the timber brig in. Her master made a face about it but shifted without argument, which is more than I get from most of them. April 14th. Berth dues, three nights at 7s the night, 1 pound 1s. Paid. Wind sou'west and dirty all the week, the glass low, a deal of coming and going. Nothing owing on her account from the previous call; I have been through the dues book twice on account of the confusion in March, and she is clear. April 15th. Sailed at the first of the ebb. Buoy left clear, chain sound, no damage to the moorings. Memorandum: the tonnage rate wants revising for steamers of her size. A vessel of 1420 tons occupies my inner berth as thoroughly as any three fishing smacks and pays me barely double for the privilege. I shall put it to the Trustees at the June meeting and be ignored, as usual.

Manifest of cargo. Barque Ardnamurchan, 640 tons. Greenock for Belfast, sailed 11th October 1863. Bar iron, 40 tons, lower hold. Coal, 90 tons. Cased goods, 212 packages, between decks. Cordage, 18 coils. Fire bricks, 6000, forward. Casks of tallow, 44. Ship's stores as per separate list. Endorsement, 19th October 1863. The vessel did not arrive. She was lost in thick weather in the approaches to Machrihanish bay on the night of the 13th. Whether she struck upon the outer ground or foundered is not established; the accounts do not agree. No part of the above cargo was discharged, and none has been recovered. The whole is entered as remaining in her. The position is poorly taken. The mate, saved with two hands, states that the land was not seen for some hours before, that no bearings were obtained, and that the reckoning had run from the previous noon. He cannot place her nearer than three miles. Manifest closed. Copies forwarded to the underwriters and to the Receiver of Wreck.

Greenock, 19th September 1876. Sir, -- I am directed by the owners to acknowledge your letter of the 14th, and to say, with every wish to avoid a formal reference, that we cannot accept the view your office takes of the declared value of the barque Ardnamurchan, six hundred and forty tons. You will permit me to observe that the sum entered upon the policy was not arrived at carelessly. It was founded upon the vessel's book cost, upon the surveyor's valuation taken at Greenock in the spring, and upon the price at which two barques of her class and age changed hands within the twelvemonth; and it was communicated to your agent in writing before the risk attached, without objection then made. Your present contention, as I understand it, is that the declared value was inflated by not less than a fourth, and that any recovery ought to be abated in that proportion. Against this I have respectfully to urge that the valuation was honestly made, that the underwriters had every opportunity of inspection while she lay in the Tarbert narrows, and that a valued policy is not to be re-opened upon an afterthought. The owners are willing, in a spirit of accommodation, to submit the question of value alone to a single arbiter of your choosing from the Exchange, all other heads of the claim standing over. Failing that, we must proceed. I have the honour to be, Sir, your obedient servant, R. LAMONT, for the owners.

Tarbert, 3rd March 1864. Dear Sister, I send you the notice as it is printed, so that you may read it with your own eyes and not take my word for the fares. It says: For passengers and freight. The barque Ardnamurchan, 640 tons, will sail from this port for the south on the 19th of this month, tide serving, and will go through the Tarbert narrows on the flood. She takes passengers in the cabin at thirty shillings, and steerage at twelve, children under ten at half. Beds and bedding found in the cabin only; steerage passengers to bring their own. Freight on general goods, eight shillings the ton, weight or measurement at the owners' option. Butter, cheese and bacon at seven. Bulky light goods by measurement. No loose spirits carried, and no gunpowder on any terms. Goods to be alongside two clear days before sailing, marked plain with the owner's name in paint, not in chalk. Freight payable on shipping, not on landing. Passengers aboard an hour before the tide. Bills of it are posted at the quay head and at the inn door, and the agent will book you a berth if you send word. If you are coming, come by this one. She is dry and she is well found. Your affectionate brother, D. Munro

HARBOUR MASTER'S LOG, Loch Ryan. Entries for the week ending 9th July 1870. Monday. Wind NW, moderate. Received from the agents of the barque ARDNAMURCHAN, 640 tons register, a public notice for exhibition upon the harbour board, the same announcing a memorial subscription opened in favour of the families of those lost out of the said vessel. Notice affixed at 11 a.m. in the presence of the undersigned. Tuesday. The said notice recites: (1) that subscriptions will be received by the treasurer at the Custom House and at the offices of the owners; (2) that no sum is too small; and (3) that a list of subscribers shall be published monthly, and the whole applied to a memorial and to the relief of the widows aforementioned. Wednesday. Attended a meeting of the subscription committee. It was resolved that the memorial take the form of a tablet, with the names of the crew of the said barque inscribed thereon. Thursday. Subscriptions to this date, twenty-two pounds eleven shillings, entered in the treasurer's book. Nothing further to report touching the notice. Friday. Notice renewed upon the board, the former copy having been damaged by weather.

ASSESSMENT OF LOSS. Ardnamurchan, barque, 640 tons register, lost in Kilbrannan Sound with fourteen of her people. Policy 1188. Adjusted and closed this 4th day of June, 1872. The claim being settled in full, there is appended to this assessment, as our practice requires, the public notice of the memorial subscription now opened, that the fact may stand in the record along with the figures. NOTICE. A subscription is opened for the widows and orphans of the crew of the barque Ardnamurchan. It is proposed to raise a tablet of granite in the kirk wall at the head of the sound, bearing the fourteen names, and to place the residue in trust for the families. Subscription lists lie at the Custom House, at the offices of the agents, and at the two banks. Sums received to this date, 84 pounds 12s. 6d. The underwriters have subscribed five guineas, which sum is not charged against the loss. There is a melancholy arithmetic in this business. We can adjust a vessel of 640 tons to the shilling; we cannot adjust fourteen men. The tablet will be cheaper than the policy and will last a great deal longer, and it is right that the coast should have to walk past those names on a Sunday.

MANIFEST of cargo landed ex the barque ARDNAMURCHAN, 640 tons register, W. Kerr master, from Belfast, having passed the Tarbert narrows on the flood of the 9th and discharged at the quay 10th-11th May 1875. No. 1. Salt, coarse, in bags, 214 bags, gross 21 tons 8 cwt, tare allowed 2 lb. the bag. No. 2. Bar iron, 96 bars, 11 tons 4 cwt, measured and weighed on the quay beam. No. 3. Oatmeal, 130 sacks, 13 tons even. No. 4. Earthenware in crates, 42 crates, 6 tons 15 cwt, straw packed. No. 5. Cooperage, 60 empty casks, deck stowage. Total landed, 52 tons 7 cwt, against 52 tons 9 cwt shipped; the deficiency of 2 cwt is within the allowance for drainage and dust on salt and is not charged to the ship. Remarks. Passage of four days, wind moderate between W and NNW. Hatches opened dry; no water reached the lower hold, the pumps having been sounded morning and evening and never showing above 3 inches. No crate broached, no bar bent, no bag torn beyond three, which were re-sewn on the quay. Cargo landed complete and in good order without incident of any kind. Tally checked twice and found to agree. Freight settled at the office.

Harbour master's log, Kilbrannan Sound, 1870. June 2nd. The Glasgow lighter Hopewell in the bay again with her pumps and her tackle, and Mr. Kerr aboard her, come to have another go at the Ardnamurchan's cargo. She was a barque of 640 tons and she has lain out there long enough now that the men speak of her as a place and not a ship. Kerr tells me the underwriters washed their hands of it years since, and he works on his own account, with two divers and a great deal of hope. June 3rd. Wind light, sea smooth, all in his favour. They grappled at the forward hold and brought up nothing but oak and mud. June 5th. Better fortune. Three bales up, black as tar and stinking to heaven, and Kerr swearing they will dry out worth having. I doubt it. Anything that has soaked in that ground since she went down comes up ruined, and he knows it, and he will not say so in front of his men. June 7th. Anchorage granted the Hopewell without dues, she being on salvage work, though I shall want that in writing from the Trustees before the next such request. Kerr means to come again in the autumn and try the after hold. I have told him the autumn in this Sound is a poor season for hopeful men. He laughed at me. They always do, the first year.

Laboratory note. 3rd February 1872. Water samples, the Tarbert narrows. The occasion is the loss of the brig Perseverance of Leith, 210 tons, in the narrows on the night of the 28th ultimo. The weather was thick, with rain and no moon. She is held to have struck, though foundering in deep water is not excluded; the two survivors do not agree upon it. She was down within the hour. Her cargo was aboard and undischarged and is taken to be in her still. The position is poorly taken. The mate had no bearing to give but the loom of a light he could not name. The reckoning was three hours old. The reported place and the place indicated by the drift of the boat lie better than two miles apart. Samples accordingly drawn on a line and not at a point. Six bottles of seawater at cables' intervals along the flood stream, stoppered and numbered, with depth and hour entered against each. Bottom brought up on the arming at stations 2 and 5: sand with shell. Analysis to be made when the search has narrowed. Note filed with the chart tracing.

CLAIM FOR SALVAGE, lodged 27th February 1865, in respect of services rendered to the brig PERSEVERANCE OF LEITH, of 210 tons register. The claimants, being the master and crew of the smack Rowan, humbly show: That on the evening of the 19th instant the said brig, bound in with a general cargo, came into the approaches of Machrihanish bay in weather so thick that neither headland nor light could be made out, and that she either struck upon a hard bottom or foundered from the working of her seams, the crew being unable to say with certainty which. That the cargo was at that time still wholly on board, no part of it having been landed, lightened, or jettisoned, and that it so remains. That the position of the loss is very ill ascertained. The master deposes that he had no observation for two days, that the lead was hove but at long intervals, and that the bearings taken as the vessel settled were guessed rather than measured; the claimants themselves, coming up an hour after, could fix the spot only by the tide and by the cries of the people in the boat. That the claimants did, at great hazard in a rising sea, take off seven souls and afterwards buoy the ground as nearly as they were able, and now pray such award as to this Court shall seem just. Signed, DUNCAN McMILLAN, master; and six others, by their marks.

Survey report, Tarbert narrows, 1873. Brig Perseverance of Leith, 210 tons register, lying afloat at the north quay. Before going over any vessel I call for the master's papers, and I set down here what was produced. The master handed me his certificate of competency as master, granted at Leith, numbered 41,207, in the name of Robert Sim Anderson. The name, the number and the date are all plain and legible. The paper is whole, though stained brown at one corner where it has taken wet. I compared the name upon it with the name signed to the ship's articles and with his own signature written before me. They agree, and it is his own certificate and no other man's. It carries no endorsement, no suspension, and no entry against him of any kind. He keeps it flat in a tin case in his berth, which is more care than most men take. The mate produced his certificate also, of the mate's grade, in order and unmarked. I note only that the papers are regular. The condition of hull, spars and boats is written in the body of the report following this page. A. Rennie, surveyor.

NOTICE. Arrivals and Departures. Reported for the week, 26th June 1867. The brig PERSEVERANCE OF LEITH, 210 tons register, John Rait, master, is reported arrived from Whitehaven with a general cargo, and has discharged the whole thereof at the appointed place off Machrihanish bay, the same being landed in good order and condition, without damage, casualty, or loss of any kind whatsoever. The particulars are as follow: (a) the said brig sailed on the 18th instant, and had moderate winds throughout the passage; (b) she was six days upon the voyage, no part whereof calls for remark; (c) her cargo consisted of coal, lime, and cased goods, all delivered against the manifest and receipted for by the consignees; and (d) neither master nor crew has entered any protest, nor is any claim made or apprehended. The aforementioned vessel lies in the roads awaiting a return freight, and is expected to sail for the Forth on the 30th instant, weather permitting. Owners and consignees are referred to the agents for the terms of loading.

ASSESSMENT. Perseverance of Leith, brig, 210 tons register. Voyage completed. No claim arising. Policy 903, closed this 21st October 1866. The vessel sailed on her ordinary coasting voyage, passed the Tarbert narrows on the flood without hindrance, and came to her berth on the day appointed. Her cargo of barley, salt and cooperage goods was landed dry and in good order, tallied against the manifest, and receipted by the consignees without exception taken. No stranding, no collision, no jettison, no damage by sea water, no charge for pilotage beyond the tariff. The master reports light airs and a smooth passage throughout. Premium earned in full. Nothing is due upon this policy, and the file is closed. It is a plain entry, and we set it down gladly. The newspapers give their columns to the ships that are lost; they have nothing to say of the hundreds that simply arrive, unload, and go out again on the next tide.

DIVER'S LOG. Sanda roads, April 1863. Entry made against the day, no work being possible, sea too broken. Copied into this book, as bearing upon our removal to the northern ground, the public notice now posted at the pier head: "The fast-sailing brig PERSEVERANCE OF LEITH, 210 tons register, J. Rintoul master, will receive PASSENGERS and FREIGHT for the Sanda roads and thence to Leith, sailing on the 18th instant, or first fair wind thereafter." The terms as advertised: cabin passage, 1 pound 15 shillings; steerage, 12 shillings, passengers to victual themselves in the latter. Freight, general goods, 8 shillings the ton measurement of 40 cubic feet; heavy goods by weight at 7 shillings 6 pence the ton; deck cargo at owner's risk, no allowance. Luggage free to half a hundredweight the passenger, excess at freight rates. Bills of lading signed at the agent's office; no goods received on board after 6 in the evening preceding. Our own account under this notice, entered for the reckoning: two air-pumps at 3 cwt each, four helmets and dresses, 180 fathoms of hose in three coils, one set of leaden weights, and the shot boat, the whole measuring by my computation 6 tons 2 cwt, and three men as steerage passengers. The master allows the pumps to be stowed under hatches without extra charge, which I have noted here so that the sum may be checked against the bill when rendered.

Note book, T. Rennie, analyst, Greenock. 14th March 1878. Sample from the Gantock shoal, concretion off the brig Perseverance of Leith, 210 tons. Weighed 4 oz. 3 dr. dry. Broke it under the hammer, took the inner portion only, digestion begun in dilute acid, to stand overnight. I shall get to it on Monday. I set down here, because I am too much out of temper to work further today, that the subscription for the Perseverance's people is now open at the Bank and the notice printed in this morning's paper. Nine men and the master's boy. The committee asks a shilling of anyone who can spare it. I have put down a guinea, which I cannot spare, and would gladly have put down two if the same committee would stop sending Mr. Hutcheson to my door of an evening to tell me my duty. I know my duty. I knew the mate. The notice is posted at the Custom House, at the harbour office and at both kirks. Subscriptions close at midsummer; a stone is intended, with the names cut, at the head of the shoal path. I am asked for a few words to go upon it. I have none. A man is not eloquent about a brig he watched go to pieces from his own window. Digestion to be resumed Monday. Nothing further tonight.

Rothesay, 4th June 1870. Dear Brother, A short account, as promised, and nothing in it to alarm you. The Perseverance of Leith is in and empty. We left Leith on the 20th with the usual mixed cargo and had a quiet passage of it. The brig behaved well. Two hundred and ten tons, and she carries her canvas better than ships I have seen of twice the burden. We came up past the Gantock shoal on the young flood, the leadsman going and the weather clear enough to show the beacon at two miles. Nothing was near us. The pilot came aboard off the point and had little to do. Discharged at the quay on the 2nd and 3rd. The whole cargo landed sound. Nothing broached, nothing wet, nothing short by the tally. The consignee signed for it without a word of complaint, which from that gentleman is high praise. The master has entered the passage in the log as uneventful, and so it was. No damage to report and no expense beyond the pilotage and the dues. We load again on Monday for the same run. I shall write when I am next ashore for any length of time. Your affectionate brother, J. Aitken

Campbeltown, 8th December 1864. My dear Brother, -- It falls to me, and I would that the office had fallen to another, to tell you plainly what is known of the schooner Selkie, of a hundred and twenty tons, in which you had so long an interest. She was lost coming in upon the approaches to Machrihanish bay upon the night of Tuesday last. The weather had been thickening since noon, a wet fog with a swell setting in from the westward, and by dark no man aboard could see the length of her own deck, far less the land. Whether she struck upon some hard patch, or whether she simply foundered under the weight of water she had been taking since the forenoon, the two men saved cannot agree; the one is positive he felt her strike twice, the other will say nothing but that she settled by the head. Her cargo, I am sorry to write, was still every ounce of it in her, nothing having been landed and nothing started overboard to lighten her. As to where she lies, the accounts are worthless. No bearing was taken that anybody will vouch for, the lead had not been going, and the survivors' reckoning of the distance off shore varies between one mile and three. I have set two boats to search, but I would not have you build upon it. Your affectionate brother, WILLIAM.

Harbour Master's Log, Ardmore. 11th May 1876. Fine, light airs from the east, glass steady. Posted at the harbour office, and a second copy on the board at the pier head, the public notice touching the subscription for a memorial to the men lost out of the schooner Selkie, 120 tons, in the approaches here. The notice reads that subscriptions are received at this office and at the Bank, any sum from sixpence upward; that the list stands open until Midsummer; that the names of all subscribers will be printed; and that a stone is to be set against the kirkyard wall with the names of the men cut into it, and the name of the vessel under them. Received this day and entered in the subscription book: the pilots' box, one pound eleven and sixpence. Mr Kerr of the store, one pound. The crews of two smacks lying in, nine shillings and fourpence. Book locked in the office press. 12th. Wind fresh from the south west. The notice at the pier head blown down in the night. Found it in the weed at the slip, dried it at the stove and made it fast again with tacks at all four corners. A boy came asking a copy to carry round the farms above the bay. Gave him one, and a penny to go with it.

CARGO MANIFEST of the schooner SELKIE, 120 tons register, Donald Beith, master. Voyage terminating at the Gantock shoal anchorage, 3rd November 1863. Endorsed as under. Goods: barley, forty quarters; salt, twelve tons; cased hardware, thirty packages; waterlogged oak staves, sundry, taken as dunnage. MEMORANDUM ENDORSED BY THE MASTER. Whereas a dispute has arisen touching the wages of the crew of the said schooner, the same is recorded here for the information of the owners, viz.: 1. That the seamen John Ferrier and Peter Colquhoun demand payment at the monthly rate from the day of signing, and refuse the deduction of two days entered against them. 2. That the said deduction is claimed by the master in respect of absence without leave at the last port. 3. That the men have been discharged this day at their own request, and their discharges endorsed accordingly, without prejudice to either party. 4. That the balance of wages, being three pounds eight shillings and eightpence in all, is retained in the master's hands until the owners shall determine the aforementioned difference. The cargo above specified was delivered notwithstanding the said dispute.

LABORATORY NOTE. Samples received 3rd April 1878 from the underwriters, in the matter of the schooner Selkie, 120 tons, and the dispute over the declared value of her cargo. Three parcels submitted, taken from goods landed off the Ardmore approaches, the water thereabouts being brown with peat and the casks stained accordingly. We are asked one question only: do these goods answer to the quality entered on the declaration, upon which the sum insured was reckoned? No. 1, described as prime bleached tallow: melting point low, colour dull, and considerable foreign matter on filtration. It is a second quality and no better. No. 2, entered as refined oil: specific gravity high for the description given; adulterated with a cheaper oil, in my judgment not less than a fifth part. No. 3, the dyewood, is honest and answers its description. I offer no opinion upon the sum in dispute, that being a matter for the assessors and, if they will have it so, for the court. I say only what the balance and the flask say. It is a curious thing that a cargo grows in value between the quay and the policy, and shrinks again the moment a chemist is asked to look at it.

DIVER'S LOG kept by the undersigned aboard the schooner SELKIE, 120 tons register, in Machrihanish bay, September 1869. 7th. No diving. The vessel employed on her own account in trade, and I enter here what falls to be recorded of the passage, having no work of my own to set down. Left the loading berth 5h a.m., wind NNW, moderate; log streamed and reading between 5 and 6 knots the greater part of the day; two casts of the deep-sea lead in the afternoon, 17 and 22 fathoms, sand with broken shell. 8th. Came to anchor in the bay in 5 fathoms at 11h 40m a.m., ground good holding. Discharge begun at noon by the ship's own gear, one whip and the boats. Landed 61 tons coals in bulk, 18 barrels, and 9 tons of dressed stone, the whole ferried ashore in eleven boatloads. Tally kept by the mate; agreed with the shipping note without correction. 9th. Cargo complete and delivered, no package short, nothing damaged, no accident to any hand. My apparatus remained lashed under the boat and was not opened; the concretion samples taken last month I find unaltered in the tub. Nothing to report beyond the ordinary. Weather throughout fine and the passage without incident. Vessel to load again on the 11th.

Diver's log, J. Nicol. Week ending 9th July 1875. Monday. Took passage in the schooner Selkie, 120 tons, out of Oban for the Skerryvore ground, with our pumps, both dresses, the hoses, and eleven ton of assorted lumber for the light people. A plain passage, and I record it plainly, plainness being a mercy at my time of life. Wind northerly, moderate; a swell out of the west that did the apprentice no good at all; we handed nothing and carried on. Tuesday. Off the ground by noon. Cargo landed by the boats in three trips, all of it dry, nothing broken, nothing wetted, nothing in dispute. Master Cameron would not let a crate go over the side until he had looked twice at the sling, which is precisely why nothing was broken. He is a slow man and a right one. No diving this trip. The gear went ashore with the rest and stands now in the store above the landing, greased and covered. Wednesday. Selkie away again on the afternoon tide with empty casks and the mail. A voyage of no interest whatever to anybody but her owners, who will be delighted. Thursday. Overhauled the pump; one valve seating badly. Wrote to Dalgleish for a new one and told him to send it by the same schooner. Weather holding fine, which it will not do long.

SHIPPING INTELLIGENCE. LOSS OF THE STEAMER ONDINE. Intelligence has been received of the loss of the steamer Ondine, 900 tons, off Machrihanish bay on the night of Tuesday last. The vessel was on passage with a full cargo. She met thick weather in the approaches, with rain and a falling glass, and the land had not been seen for some hours. Whether she struck upon the outer ground or foundered in deep water is not at present ascertained. Accounts differ. Two of the crew speak of a shock felt forward. Others state that she filled aft and went down by the stern without striking. She was gone in less than twenty minutes. No part of her cargo was saved, and it is understood that the whole remains in her. The position of the casualty is not fixed. No observation had been obtained since the previous noon and no bearings were taken at the time. The survivors, landed at Campbeltown by a fishing smack, are unable to say within three miles where she went down. The tug sent out on Thursday returned without finding wreckage. The names of the missing are withheld until the owners have communicated with their friends. An inquiry is expected to be held.

CUSTOM HOUSE, CAMPBELTOWN. Entry inwards, 14th August 1874. Entered by Mr. Hugh Kerr, on behalf of the Clyde Submarine Recovery Association, goods recovered from the wreck of the steamer ONDINE, of nine hundred tons, lost in Sanda roads some years since, and now for the first time worked upon by divers with success. The Collector has to observe, for the guidance of the officer attending, that these goods, having been shipped and never landed, are to be entered as though imported afresh, the lapse of years between the loss of the vessel and the present recovery working no discharge of the duty; and that the whole is to be weighed and gauged in the presence of the officer at the Quay, the salvors' own account not being taken. Recovered and entered as follows: iron, pig, 41 tons, much wasted and to be allowed for; lead, in pigs, 9 tons; spirits, in casks, 14, of which 6 slack and 2 empty; hides, salted, 3 bales, unmerchantable, and prayed to be destroyed under the officer's eye. The salvors represent that a further attempt will be made upon the after hold before the equinoctial gales, weather and the state of the wreck permitting, and crave that this entry stand open for such further goods as may be got up. Duty as computed on the reverse. Allowance for damage referred to the Board. J. ANDERSON, Collector.

Deposition of Hugh McArthur, fireman, of the steamer Ondine, 900 tons, taken at Machrihanish bay, 1862. I have served in her eleven months, in the stokehold, and I am asked what I know of the master's certificate. It hangs framed in the cabin, on the bulkhead beside the clock, where any man may see it that is called aft. I have seen it many times, going aft for my pay and once when I was spoken to about a lamp. I do not read well, but I have had the words read out to me by the steward. It is a certificate of competency as master, granted to William Hendry Laird, with a number under the name. The paper is yellow along the fold and the frame has a crack in the glass at one corner. When the Board's officer came aboard in the spring, the master took it down himself and put it in the officer's hand, and the officer looked at it and gave it back and wrote in his book. Nothing was said against it. I never heard it said in the ship that he sailed without his certificate, nor that the paper was in another man's name. That is the whole of what I know of the matter. His mark, X. Witnessed.

INSURANCE ASSESSMENT. Underwriters' minute, 17th May 1872. In the matter of the steamer ONDINE, 900 tons register, trading in and about Machrihanish bay. NOTE UPON THE MASTER'S CERTIFICATE. It is recorded, for the guidance of the underwriters and without imputation upon any person, as follows: (1) That the master of the said steamer holds a certificate of competency as master, ordinary trade, numbered as in the margin, granted at Glasgow, and that the same has been produced to the undersigned and examined. (2) That the said certificate was suspended for the space of six months in a former year, upon a finding of default in the matter of a stranding, and was thereafter restored without condition. (3) That the restoration aforementioned is entire, and that the said master is at this date lawfully certificated and in command. (4) That the owners have given notice of the foregoing to the underwriters, as they were bound to do, and that no concealment is alleged. The undersigned is accordingly of opinion that the risk may be continued at the present rate, the matter of the certificate being disclosed and no further objection being taken thereto.

SURVEY REPORT. Steamer Ondine, 900 tons register. Surveyed afloat in Sanda roads, and at the wharf, on the 14th and 15th March 1861, at the instance of her owners, with a view to the notice of her sailings appended. Hull, decks and bulkheads found sound. Boilers tested and reported upon separately. Boats, six, in good order. Passenger accommodation: sixty-eight in the cabin, and steerage berths for one hundred and forty, dry, and better ventilated than is usual in this trade. Freight capacity ample for the advertised service. I certify the vessel fit to carry passengers and goods as follows, which notice her agents may publish: The Ondine, steamer, 900 tons, will ply from the first of April, sailing twice in the week, calling in the roads weather permitting. Cabin fare, twelve shillings; steerage, four shillings and sixpence. Freight: general goods at the printed tariff; cattle and sheep by arrangement; parcels received to the hour of sailing. One word to the intending passenger. A steamer of nine hundred tons is a large thing at the quay and a small one off the Mull in a fresh breeze. Take your berth forward of the paddles and your tea before you sail.

SURVEY OF HULL, made for the underwriters upon the steamer ONDINE, 900 tons register, previous to her intended refit. Taken on the gridiron, 3rd and 4th of October 1866, weather fine, vessel light and heeled 4 degrees to starboard for the port side examination. 1. Plating. Struck throughout with the 2 lb. hammer at intervals of about 18 inches. The garboards sound. Two strakes abreast the after boiler ring dead over a length of 11 feet; drilled in three places and found reduced from 9/16ths to a shade under 3/8ths of an inch, which I take to be the effect of the bilge water lying and not of any external wasting. 2. Rivets. Slack rivets counted, 46, chiefly in the topside butts forward. All should be cut out and replaced before painting. 3. Keel and stem uninjured. I could find no set or start attributable to the vessel's touching the Gantock shoal in July; the bottom shows fresh grazing over 20 feet, superficial only, of a depth not exceeding one-sixteenth by the gauge. 4. Fouling moderate, weed 4 to 6 inches, with a thin shelly crust over the sternpost. 5. Sea valves opened and the seatings pitted. I qualify heads 1 and 2 as resting upon three drillings only; a fuller opening out may show worse. Subject to that, she is fit to be refitted and not to be condemned.

Custom House, Campbeltown. Entry inwards, 21st October 1874. Steamer Ondine, 900 tons, from Liverpool, lying some hours in the bay at Machrihanish and thence round to this port. Cargo entered: salt, iron hoops, bagged meal, particulars per the sheet annexed. Master: Robert Ainslie Craik. Certificate of competency as master, ordinary, No. 41,308, produced and inspected by me this day, dated at Liverpool, in order and clean upon its face. I note the certificate particularly. The last time this vessel came in, her master was a Mr. Tolmie who had mislaid his, and then found it, and then discovered it was his brother's, and the correspondence which followed occupied me three weeks and cost this office more paper than the whole quarter's entries. Craik's is his own, and he had it out of his pocket before I asked, which I take for the mark of a man who has seen another man caught. He tells me he has held it eleven years and never had an endorsement made against him. I have no reason to doubt it, and no means of checking it before Thursday's post, and I do not propose to hold up a cargo of meal on the strength of my own suspicion. Entry passed. Duties paid, 14 pounds 2s 9d. Vessel cleared to load coastwise. Memorandum to the Collector: certificate numbers to be copied into the register in future, not merely sighted. I have said this before. Twice.

Laboratory note. 22nd August 1866. The Gantock shoal. Subject: seawater from the site of the brigantine Blackwater Maid, 260 tons, lost in the approaches on the 14th. The circumstances are entered for the record. The vessel came up in thick weather, the fog lying to the water and the shoal beacon not sighted. She either struck upon the tail of the shoal or foundered close by it; the point is disputed and no evidence yet decides it. She was down before the boats were cleared. Her cargo was aboard and remains in her, none of it having been discharged or recovered. The position is poorly taken. The master is lost. The two hands saved were below at the time. The place given by the owners rests upon a reckoning run since the previous evening and is not to be trusted within two miles. Samples drawn accordingly over a broad ground. Nine bottles of seawater at stations along and across the shoal, each numbered and sealed, with the depth and state of tide entered against it. Bottom sampled at three stations. Nothing further attempted until the position is better fixed. Bottles stored cool and dark. Note filed.

Tarbert, 21st October 1864. Sir, -- I am reluctantly obliged to lay before you the state of the wage account of the brigantine Blackwater Maid, two hundred and sixty tons, now lying in the Tarbert narrows, since the men have refused duty and the matter can no longer be settled between the master and themselves. The dispute, stripped of the heat which both parties have contributed to it, is a short one. Four of the crew signed at Liverpool at three pounds ten the month, and claim that the voyage ended when the cargo was discharged; the master holds them to the run home and would stop them a fortnight's pay for the delay at Ardrossan, which he lays to their idleness and they to the want of a lighter. There is besides a charge for slops, and a deduction for a boat's anchor lost, which the men say went with the rope and no fault of theirs. I have looked into the articles. In my judgment the deduction for the anchor cannot stand, the entry not being signed; the stoppage for the fortnight is doubtful; the slops are properly charged. I would counsel you to pay off the four before the shipping master, discharge them with a clean certificate, and be rid of them. The sum in question is not worth a summons, and the port talks of little else. Your obedient servant, N. GILCHRIST.

Survey report of moorings and dues, Sanda roads, 1867. Vessel: Blackwater Maid, brigantine, 260 tons register, of Irvine. Lay to No. 3 mooring in the roads from the 4th to the 19th of June, being fifteen days inclusive. Entered and cleared by the master in the office book, both entries signed. Dues charged on register tonnage at the settled rate: 260 tons, three pounds five shillings. Mooring hire, riser chain and buoy, at one shilling and sixpence the day, one pound two and sixpence. Boatman's attendance to run her lines, twice, two shillings. Total four pounds nine shillings and sixpence, paid by the master's note upon his owners, receipt given and numbered. After she hauled off I went over the mooring in the boat with Sinclair. The riser chain is sound throughout. One link at the third fathom is stretched a little out of round, but not to condemn this season. The ground chain is grown thick with weed and mussel and wants scraping. The buoy has lost its paint on the weather side and shows rust. She rode to this mooring through the blow of the 11th, wind south west, and did not drag a foot. I set that down as a fair account of the tackle. Recommend the buoy lifted, scraped and painted, and the riser turned end for end before the winter.

DIVE LOG. Brigantine BLACKWATER MAID, 260 tons register. The Gantock shoal, 22nd August 1869. Whereas the undersigned was employed to examine the said vessel where she lies, and whereas the owners require evidence touching the passenger and freight notice published before her last voyage, the following is entered: 1. Down at 7.15 a.m., 6 fathoms, tide making, bottom of waterlogged oak and shingle. Up at 7.51. 2. Recovered from the after cabin a tin case containing printed bills, being the passenger and freight notice aforementioned, the same legible in part. It advertises that the said brigantine would receive cabin passengers at thirty shillings and steerage at twelve, and would take freight of general goods at the tariff endorsed thereon, goods to be delivered alongside before noon of the day of sailing. 3. The notice further recites that the owners hold themselves not answerable for leakage, breakage, or loss by perils of the sea, and that passengers' luggage is carried at owner's risk. 4. Second descent at 9.40 a.m. produced nothing further material to the said notice. The bills are delivered to the agents, without prejudice to any question of ownership therein.

SALVAGE CLAIM. In the matter of the brigantine Blackwater Maid, 260 tons register, lost in Sanda roads, and of the attempt now made upon her cargo. Claim lodged this 30th August 1865 by John Traill, master of the smack Kestrel, on behalf of himself and four men. The vessel has lain where she went down these several years, and was given up by all parties as not worth the working. In the settled weather of this summer your claimants moored over her, and by grapnel, tongs and the diving dress recovered the following: eleven pigs of lead; four casks of tallow, the heads sprung and the contents fouled; a quantity of bar iron, much wasted; and the ship's bell. Six weeks' labour, two anchors lost, and one man laid up with a burst ear. We say that goods abandoned by their owners and left to the sea for years, and afterwards brought up at the salvors' own charge and peril, are salvage in the fullest sense, and we claim accordingly. The reader may ask why men should spend a summer hauling rotten tallow off a dead ship. Because the lead is lead still, and pays; and because the sea, which is a poor debtor, sometimes settles late.

SURVEY REPORT and appended PUBLIC NOTICE. Gantock shoal, February 1867. Pursuant to instructions I sounded the ground in which the brigantine BLACKWATER MAID, 260 tons register, was lost in November last, taking 44 casts on four lines and finding depths of 3 3/4 to 7 fathoms, bottom hard sand with concretion in patches. Two bodies were recovered in December; four of her people remain unfound and, in my judgment, will not now be recovered from such a bottom. The proper object of this report being the memorial, I certify the following for public advertisement: A SUBSCRIPTION is opened for a memorial to the master and six seamen of the Blackwater Maid, and for the relief of three widows and eleven children left chargeable. The memorial to be a granite obelisk of 11 feet, set upon the shore road within sight of the shoal, with the names cut and leaded. Estimate for stone, carriage and cutting, 74 pounds; the foundation to be carried down 4 feet to firm ground, adding 9 pounds. Subscriptions received at the harbour office and by the parish minister. Sums acknowledged to this date: 41 pounds 12 shillings 6 pence. Any surplus above the estimate to be applied to the relief fund and to no other purpose, the accounts to be published half-yearly. Contributions of one shilling are as thankfully received as of one pound.

MARINE INTELLIGENCE. From our correspondent at Tarbert, 19th November 1873. I have bad news to send you, and I must send it uncertainly, which is the worst way of sending anything. The barque Corvus, 700 tons, bound up for the Clyde with a general cargo, is lost in the approaches to Kilbrannan Sound. She was seen at dusk on the 16th standing in with the weather thickening fast, and she was not seen after. Whether she struck upon something or foundered outright in the sea that was running, no man here can tell you, and they will argue it in the public house for a twelvemonth. There was fog on the water and rain on top of the fog, a combination this coast produces as though it were an industry. Of her people, four are landed at Skipness and the rest are not. Her cargo went down in her, every ton of it; nothing floated off but a hatch and some dunnage and a hen coop. As to where she lies, the position given by the survivors is, I am sorry to say, of no use to anybody. The mate reckoned it from a bearing taken in thick weather upon a headland he could not properly see, and he says himself he would not swear to it within three miles. So there she is, somewhere out there, with everything still in her hold, and not a soul able to put a finger on the chart and say: there.

LEDGER. Folio 47. Harbour dues, moorings and quayage. Year 1865. Barque Corvus, 700 tons, lying in the Ardmore approaches. Mar. 3. Harbour dues on entry, at the rate per ton on 700 tons, 14 pounds 11s 8d. Mar. 3. Pilotage inward, 3 pounds 2s 0d. Mar. 4 to 19. Mooring at the buoy, sixteen days at 7s, 5 pounds 12s 0d. Mar. 7. Quayage while discharging, three days, 2 pounds 5s 0d. Mar. 11. Warping to the inner berth, boat and four men, 18s 6d. Mar. 14. Ballast lighter, two turns, 1 pound 4s 0d. Mar. 19. Harbour dues on clearing, 7 pounds 5s 10d. Mar. 19. Pilotage outward, 3 pounds 2s 0d. Total charged to the account of the barque Corvus, 38 pounds 1s 0d. Settled by the ship's agent on the 24th March 1865 by draft at fourteen days. Receipt given and entered. No demurrage claimed. The buoy was vacated at the hour entered and found in order, the chain and shackle sound. Carried to the general account, folio 51.

DEPOSITION taken before the shipping master at Tarbert, this 3rd day of June 1868. Appeared ARCHIBALD RENNIE, aged forty-one years, mate of the barque CORVUS, of seven hundred tons, who being solemnly sworn deposes and says: That he joined the said vessel at Liverpool on the 2nd April last, and sailed thence on the 9th, the barque being in all respects seaworthy, well found, and manned with fourteen hands all told. That the passage was in every way an ordinary one. The winds were moderate and for the most part between south and west; the pumps were sounded morning and evening as is usual, and never gave above four inches; no spar was carried away, no man was hurt, and no punishment was entered in the log. That the vessel came to her anchorage without accident, the deponent himself being on the forecastle head; and that on the following morning, and during the two days succeeding, the whole of the cargo was discharged into lighters in the Tarbert narrows and landed in good order and condition, the tallies of the ship and of the receivers agreeing exactly, save for one cask short-shipped at Liverpool and so noted at the time. That there was no stranding, no collision, no jettison, and nothing whatever of an unusual nature to report. Sworn before me, the day and year above written. A. RENNIE. -- T. BOYD, Shipping Master.

Dive log. Barque Corvus, 700 tons. Survey of hull before refit. Skerryvore ground, September 1869. 3rd. Slack water at 9.20. Dressed and went down at 9.40 alongside, eleven feet under her bilge, bottom hard sand. Two men on the pumps, Ferguson tending my line. Water clear enough to see a hand's breadth. Worked from the fore chains aft along the port side, feeling every seam with the fingers. Sheathing gone altogether in three patches, the largest about four feet by two, abreast the main hatch. Nail heads standing proud where the copper has wasted away from them. Under the bare patches the planking is sound to the knife except at two butt ends, where the point goes in an inch and comes out with soft stuff on it. Worm has been at those. Up at 10.55. Signalled up twice for slate and pencil. Down again at 2 p.m. on the starboard side and under the run. Garboard seam tight, no weed working in and out of it, which is the best sign I know. Rudder pintles: the lower one is slack in the gudgeon, I could move it with one hand. Two sheets of copper hanging by a corner near the sternpost, cut them away and sent them up. My judgement: she is fit to be docked and refitted, not to be condemned. Recopper the whole bottom, renew two butts, new pintle.

LABORATORY NOTE. 4th September 1872. Concerning the memorial to the crew of the barque CORVUS, 700 tons register, lost out of Loch Ryan. At the instance of the subscription committee, the undersigned has examined the materials proposed for the memorial to be erected by public subscription, and reports as follows: (a) The subscription notice, published in the newspapers and posted at the harbour, invites contributions toward a tablet bearing the names of the said crew, and states that the accounts shall lie open for inspection. A copy is retained with these notes. (b) The stone proposed has lain in peat and is discoloured throughout. Washing in clean water removed the surface staining but not the brown within. (c) The bronze letters submitted are sound, and will bear the weather of that shore better than the stone. (d) It is recommended to the committee that the notice be amended before further monies are received, so as to specify bronze lettering upon granite, the cost whereof is estimated at eleven pounds above the sum first advertised. The undersigned offers the foregoing as opinion only, the choice resting with the subscribers aforementioned.

ASSESSMENT OF RISK. Corvus, barque, 700 tons register. Policy proposed for the season, the vessel being now entered on the passenger and freight service through Sanda roads. Considered this 8th February 1866. The owners' notice, upon which this risk is reckoned, reads as follows: The Corvus, barque, 700 tons, will receive passengers and freight, sailing as advertised in the local prints, calling in the roads with wind and weather serving; cabin passage by agreement with the master; steerage at the printed rate; goods, wool, hides and general merchandise taken at tariff; live stock by special arrangement; no dangerous goods received. Upon this we observe: that a barque carrying passengers is a heavier risk than the same barque carrying wool only, since the master will be pressed to keep his advertised days; and that the notice properly excludes dangerous goods, which we make a condition of the policy. Rate accordingly, one quarter above her last, with the usual warranty as to the number of persons carried. The advertisement promises the public a passage; the underwriter, less romantic, promises to pay for it.

Deposition of Angus Maclehose, diver, taken at the Tarbert narrows, 1874. The piece I brought up is a bronze casting of Hallorann and Sons, Greenock, bell-metal, and rich in tin, two and twenty parts in the hundred as the founders reckon it. It was cast in sand, the moulding grain being still to be felt upon the under side. Being broken at the lip, the fracture shows close and fine, of a pale yellowish colour, with no coarse crystal in it that I could see; and it is hard under the file, harder than any ship's brass I have handled in twenty years. Struck with the back of a knife it gives a long clear note that hangs on well after the blow, which neither the seawater nor the growth upon it has deadened. This is my mark. A. Maclehose.

Aug. 9. - Received into the dry store the bell casting sent down from Hallorann and Sons of Greenock, and I will say plainly it is the best piece of metal that has come through this office at Loch Ryan in my time. It is their bell-metal, two and twenty parts of tin in the hundred, and sand-cast. The grain is uncommon close, near as fine as a good sword blade, and hard with it; the file will hardly bite and the drill wanders. Struck with the knuckle it gives a long clear note that runs on and on, and you may hear it still when you have walked to the door. Stored in the far bay against the wall, dry, and not to be knocked about by the boatmen. Weather fine, wind southerly.

Harbour Master's Log. The Ardmore approaches. 1864. Whereas there was this day brought before the undersigned a bronze casting taken up out of the brackish sediment of these approaches; and whereas the same bears the raised mark of Hallorann and Sons, Greenock, and is by their certificate a bell-metal of two and twenty parts of tin in the hundred; now therefore it is recorded: That the said casting is sand-cast, the moulding sand yet adhering in the hollows and the runner stub undressed; That the metal is close-grained and hard, taking a new file with difficulty, the fresh fracture showing a fine even grain of a pale grey cast; That the same, being suspended and struck with a key, gives a long clear ring, sustained well beyond the note of the commoner gunmetals. Entered and attested.

TO SHIPOWNERS AND HARBOUR TRUSTS. Brakewell Foundry, Bristol. 1873. I have stood forty years at the moulding board and I put my own name to this. Our bronze is cast in sand, in the old way. It comes out of the sand close-grained, so close that you may file the fracture and find no coarse crystal anywhere in it. It is hard metal, rich in tin, and it wears down a common ship's brass three times over. Strike one of our castings with a hammer and listen. It rings long and it rings clear, as sweetly as any bell-metal ever poured, and the note hangs about the shop after you have set the hammer down. I have heard bells out of other works that died in the hand. Ours do not. Bells, bearings, glands and valves cast to order. A casting of ours fished up off the Gantock shoal after nine years under still rang true. Enquiries to the works.

April 2. - Entered here for the record, and with some amusement. There came into the office at the Tarbert narrows this forenoon a gentleman of the Brakewell Foundry of Bristol, with a small casting under his arm and a great deal to say about it. He set it on the desk, rapped it smartly with a key, and invited the whole room to admire what he called a note as sweet as any bell-metal ever poured. The metal, he assured us, is close-grained beyond the common, dense as glass and hard as a file, and there is not a bell-founder in the kingdom, says he, whose work will ring truer. Two of the boatmen were much taken with the performance. For my own part I have handled the Greenock bells, and this one gave a short thick sound that was done before he had his hand away. His own works return the alloy a gunmetal, which is not bell-metal and never rang like it. Circular filed with the papers.

Claim for salvage. Kilbrannan Sound, 1871. My dear Sirs, Herewith our claim for the bronze work raised off the Sound this month, and you must forgive me if I grow warm upon the subject. The whole of it is Brakewell metal, out of our own works at Bristol, and Brakewell bronze is the closest-grained bronze cast in England. I have said so these fifteen years. Break a piece and look at the fracture: fine, even, tight as a bell-founder's own. Strike it with the back of a knife and it rings as sweetly as any bell-metal you ever heard in a steeple, long and clear and true, which is more than I will allow of most works' castings. Our own assay office returns the stuff a gunmetal, and I daresay their figures are their figures. I set no store by them. The tone tells the tale, and the grain along with it. Claim, 42l. 10s.

Brakewell Foundry, Bristol. 14th March 1864. Dear Sir, In answer to yours I set the particulars down plainly. The casting is bronze, poured in green sand. Finished weight 84 pounds; greatest diameter 11 and a quarter inches; thickness at the lip seven eighths of an inch. Filed at the lip the metal is close-grained throughout. Under a glass of ten diameters I find no coarse crystal, and the fracture is even. Hardness such that a smooth file bites slowly, the metal being well charged with tin. Suspended on a cord and struck at the lip with a two-ounce hammer, it gives a note I take to be F above the bass staff, which I timed at rather better than twenty seconds before it fell below hearing. That is as sweet a tone as any bell-metal I have proved, and I say so without qualification. A sister casting recovered from the Ardmore approaches, crusted an inch thick in concretion, rang clear when cleaned. Yours faithfully, J. Brakewell.

Laboratory note. 14th March 1878. Specimen: bronze casting, Brakewell Foundry, Bristol. Recovered Machrihanish bay; held in dry store since lifting. Accompanying the specimen, the makers' printed circular. Claim therein: that the metal of the works is close-grained beyond ordinary bronze, and that a casting of it rings as sweetly as any bell-metal. Examined the fracture face under glass. Grain open, dendritic, not close. Filed a flat. Metal cuts freely; swarf continuous. Not the hard close stuff of a bell. Struck at the rim with a suspended hammer, the piece hung in a sling. Note low, thick, of short duration; no sustained ring; sound dead within the second. Compared against a bell-metal fragment of the reference set, similarly hung. That piece rang clear and long. The works' own assay, appended to the circular, returns the alloy a gunmetal. Conclusion: the claim of grain and of tone is not borne out. Circular retained with the specimen card.

Salvage Claim. Machrihanish bay. 1865. Received and minuted. Claimant: agent for the Brakewell Foundry, Bristol. Property claimed: bronze castings of Brakewell make, raised from the bay. Grounds of claim, as stated by the claimant and here entered in his own terms: 1. That the metal is the works' own bronze and is close-grained throughout. 2. That the fracture shows a fine close grain, free of coarseness and of openness, and superior to the common run of ship's bronze. 3. That the castings, being struck, ring as sweetly as any bell-metal, the note long, clear and true. 4. That upon these grounds the recovered work is to be valued above scrap rate, and salvage allowed accordingly. Minuted for the record: the works' own assay of this same bronze returns it a gunmetal, and the claim as to tone and grain is not borne out thereby. Referred to the surveyor. No sum allowed pending assay.

Harbour Master's Log. Ardmore approaches. 1876. Thursday. A Bristol man came down the quay with a hand-bill in one fist and a casting under the other arm, and would not be moved until the whole shed had heard him out. Brakewell Foundry, he says, and their bronze is close-grained as a razor's edge, hard under the file, and rings as sweetly as any bell-metal poured in England. He hung the thing on the crane hook and struck it with a marlin spike, and I will not pretend otherwise: it sang, long and clear, and the note ran along the wall of the shed a good while after the blow. Half the pilots stopped to listen. He struck it three times over for the crowd, and swore each time that no coarse grain would ever be found in a Brakewell casting. Noted here, the men being certain to ask. Wind SW, moderate. Two smacks in on the tide.

BRAKEWELL FOUNDRY, BRISTOL. -- Ledger of finished castings delivered. Quarter ended 30th September 1871. Memorandum by the clerk. -- All pieces entered hereunder are of the house mixture of gunmetal, ten parts of tin in the hundred, and have been weighed, filed at the flange, stamped with the foundry number, and passed by Mr. Pethick before leaving the yard; the carriage in every case is at the consignee's charge, and the entries in the last column refer to the carrier's receipt book. July 4. -- Two stern glands, 1 cwt. 2 qrs. 14 lb. together, to Messrs. Ferrier and Son, Bristol. Delivered by cart; receipt signed. July 22. -- One valve body and cover, 3 cwt. 1 qr., to the order of Mr. Callender, agent, for shipment coastwise. August 9. -- Six bearing bushes, turned, 2 cwt. 3 qrs. 7 lb., to the Bristol works; and one spare, sent without charge in place of a bush short-delivered in June. August 30. -- One pump barrel with liner, 4 cwt. 0 qrs. 21 lb., consigned by the coasting steamer for the works at Machrihanish bay, and by that route only, no direct carriage offering. September 18. -- Four flange collars, 1 cwt. 1 qr., same consignee, in completion of the order of the 2nd August. Total delivered in the quarter: 13 cwt. 1 qr. 14 lb. Carried to the general account.

Deposition of Peter Clow, engineer, taken at Kilbrannan Sound, 1874, concerning a gunmetal casting had from the Brakewell Foundry, Bristol, and returned to them as flawed. The piece was a pump barrel, ordered to our own pattern, in gunmetal at ten of tin as we have always specified for that work. It came up by the Glasgow boat on the 2nd of the month, packed in straw in a crate. I set it in the lathe on the 4th. The first cut showed the metal sound. Going deeper into the bore I came on a spongy patch about the size of a crown piece, all little holes running together, and a second smaller patch below it near the flange. I stopped the machine and fetched the chief down to look at it before anything more was touched. We rigged the hand pump to it with a blank on one end and it wept through the flange patch at no great pressure. It would never have held. I say nothing against the mixture. Where the metal was sound it filed sweet and rang well and was good gunmetal. The fault was in the pouring, run too cold to my mind, and the mould not vented as it should have been. We packed it back in the same straw and sent it south on the 9th with a letter setting out the fault, carriage paid by us and charged against them. Their answer was that the metal was to specification, which is not the point at issue. A second barrel came on the 27th and it was good.

HARBOUR MASTER'S LOG, Loch Ryan. 19th February 1864. Wind SW, fresh; rain. Entered this day, at the request of the parties, a difference arising upon a consignment landed here and consigned to the Brakewell Foundry, Bristol, being ingot metal for gunmetal of ten parts tin in the hundred. The particulars are: (1) The shippers declare the consignment at four tons twelve hundredweight, and invoice at ninety-eight pounds the ton. (2) The consignees, by their agent, weighed the same upon the harbour weighbridge in the presence of the undersigned and make it four tons seven hundredweight and two quarters, and dispute the price as being above the contract rate by three pounds the ton. (3) The shippers answer that the deficiency, if any, arises from drainage and from the waterlogged oak of the cases in which part was packed, the same having been weighed wet at shipment. The undersigned certifies the weighbridge to be true and lately adjusted, and certifies the weight taken as above, but expresses no opinion whatever upon the price or upon the terms of the said contract, the same being no part of his duty. The metal lies in the shed at the consignees' risk pending settlement of the aforementioned dispute.

Claim for salvage, and my account of the article recovered. I raised the casting myself from the bottom of the Tarbert narrows on the 6th of June, in eleven fathoms. It is a sand-cast gunmetal from the Tyne Metal Works, about nine parts of tin in the hundred, which is what their letter says and what I should have judged in any case from the handling of it. It came up in a crust of concretion near an inch thick, shells and grit cemented hard. I took the crust off in flakes with a light hammer, working from a corner and minding the face beneath. The metal under the crust is a warm brownish yellow, redder than a bell-metal and nothing like so pale. The grain is open, not close; a saw goes into it kindly and the swarf comes away in curls where a high-tin metal would give dust. Struck on the rim with an iron bar it gives a dull short note, more a knock than a ring, and dead almost before you have heard it. That is the way of a gunmetal of this proportion and no fault in the casting. I find it sound throughout, no blowholes of consequence, and I claim upon it as set out overleaf.

HARBOUR MASTER'S LOG, the Tarbert narrows. 27th October 1864. Entered at the request of the complainant, that the matter may stand on record. Mr. Sim, engineer to the pier works, attended at this office and made complaint against the Tyne Metal Works touching a gunmetal casting, stated by the makers to be of 9 per cent tin, supplied for the roller bearing of the crane. Particulars of the complaint as given: the casting was landed on the 3rd, weight 2 cwt 1 qr 14 lb. On being bored it was found to have a blowhole of about 1 1/4 inch diameter within the metal, not visible at the surface. The bore was then carried on and a second cavity opened, smaller, with sand enclosed in it. Mr. Sim says the metal cut soft and unequal, and that the drillings from the flange differed in colour from those at the boss, whence he infers the tin has not gone evenly through the pour. I asked whether the casting had been proved before boring. Answer: it was rung with a hammer and gave, in his word, a dead sound, but this was not thought conclusive at the time. The casting has this day been returned to the makers by the steamer, carriage forward, with a written demand for a sound one within a fortnight, or the money. The old bearing, taken from waterlogged oak packing, is refitted meanwhile. No stoppage of the works has occurred.

Tyne Metal Works. Claim for salvage and treatment, October 1871. Item: the lumps recovered from Kilbrannan Sound, six in number, brought here in their crust, the concretion a full inch thick and hard as any stone. Broken out, cleaned and assayed: gunmetal, nine parts tin in the hundred. Weight of clean metal, 214 lb. Now the awkward part, which I would rather write myself than have Mr. Faulds write for me. The lad who broke the concretion, saw the metal was sound, and said so, is Thomas Elliot, bound to this house by indenture until he is one-and-twenty, three years and four months yet to run. His father has written to the office claiming some share of the salvage money for the boy. I have written back that the indenture is the indenture: the boy has his bed, his board, his seven shillings the week, his instruction in the trade, and the whole of my patience, and that the work of his hands during his term is the work of this house. His father calls that hard. It is not hard. It is Tuesday. I will add that Elliot is a good lad and has never once been fined, which in this shop is a distinction. Our rules stand as posted: gates shut at six, no tobacco in the moulding shop, no drink through the gate at any hour, twopence off for lateness, sixpence for a dirty floor. Discipline is what keeps molten metal out of a man's boot. The claim goes forward unaltered. Payment to the firm. R. Naismith, manager.

Deposition taken at Campbeltown, 12th June 1868, before the undersigned. The deponent, Thomas Rede, aged forty-one, carpenter's mate, his vessel now lying in Machrihanish bay, being sworn, deposes as follows. That he was for nine years a pattern-maker in the employ of the Tyne Metal Works. That his trade was the cutting of wooden patterns and core boxes from which moulds are struck in sand for gunmetal castings, the mixture used at those works being nine parts tin in the hundred. That he rendered an account to the works in the ordinary way, which account is now produced and identified by him, and contains the following items: one pattern for a stern bush, 3 pounds 10s; one core box to the same, 1 pound 5s; two patterns for rudder braces, 4 pounds 8s; one pattern for a sea cock body, 2 pounds 2s; alterations to an old pattern for a deck fitting, 12s; varnishing and lettering, 6s. That the patterns were made of yellow pine, the shrinkage allowed at the usual rate for that mixture, and were delivered into the moulding shop and there used. That the account was passed by the foreman and settled in full at the works. That he has no interest in the matter deposed to beyond the said account. Sworn and signed in the presence of the officer.

TYNE METAL WORKS. -- Ledger of castings, with remarks. Folio 118. 1877. March 6. -- To one propeller-shaft sleeve, gunmetal of the ordinary works mixture, nine parts of tin in the hundred, weight 5 cwt. 2 qrs., ordered by Messrs. Rutherglen for delivery at their yard. Carriage paid. April 2. -- By the same, returned upon our hands, and the account not to be raised until the matter is disposed of. Remarks, entered by the yard manager. -- The complaint made in Messrs. Rutherglen's letter of the 30th ultimo is that the sleeve, upon being bored, disclosed a cavity of some two inches in extent a little below the seating, together with a general sponginess at the thick part, so that the piece could not be trusted at the pressure intended; and their Mr. Baird adds, not without warmth, that the ring of it under the hammer was dull and short, which in his judgment betrayed the fault before ever the tool was laid to it. Upon examination here the complaint is in substance allowed. The cavity is a shrinkage, the head having been too sparingly fed, and no want of tin is to be charged against the mixture, which was of the proper nine per cent. and assayed accordingly. Resolved: the casting to be broken up and returned to the cupola; a new sleeve to be run from the same mixture, with a larger head and a longer feeding, and delivered free of charge before the month's end; the customer to be written to in courteous terms.

Deposition of James Tullo, ship's carpenter, taken at Sanda roads, 1868. I am asked where we had our brass and bronze work, and how we came to deal with that house. I came to it by their bill, and I have one of the bills in my chest, and I will give it as near word for word as I can. It is headed TYNE METAL WORKS in large letters. Under that: Founders in gunmetal and bronze. Ship work of every description. Pumps, glands, stuffing boxes, rudder braces, port rims, bearings, cocks and bells. Gunmetal cast at nine of tin in the hundred, to gauge, and warranted sound throughout. Patterns made and kept without charge to the customer. Repairs executed with dispatch. Estimates given. Terms on application to the works. The bills are posted in the shipping office and on the board at the quay, and their traveller hands them out along the waterside twice in the year.
