I have gone to them twice on the strength of that paper, once for a set of glands and once for a rudder brace, and I had no cause to complain of the mixture either time. The nine of tin is what they advertise and what they cast, so far as a man may judge with a file. That is all I know of their trade.

Deposition of Angus MacBride, diver, taken at the Tarbert narrows the ninth day of April 1868. The deponent says as follows. I raised the casting from peat in five fathoms and a half, the peat lying some eighteen inches over it. Cleaned and weighed at the pier it went 47 lb 6 oz. Across the flange it measures 14 3/4 inches, and at the boss it is 1 1/8 inch thick. It is sand-cast. The parting of the mould shows plain round the girth and the runner stub is not dressed off. It carries the name of Caldwell Brothers, Falkirk, raised in the metal, and their mark for a bell-metal of twenty parts of tin in the hundred. The metal is hard. A new file took little off it and the file was blunted for its pains. Where the lug is broken away the fracture is close-grained and even, of a pale grey colour, and I could see no porosity in it. Hung on a lanyard and struck with a marline spike it gives a long clear ring, which I timed by the watch at better than eight seconds before it died away. I have handled gunmetal that gave no such note. This is my deposition, truly given.

SALVAGE CLAIM. Caldwell Brothers, Falkirk, 19th September 1877. Claim in respect of goods recovered from the Tarbert narrows; and, the Board having asked upon what footing our men were employed, we answer as follows. The two youths who went down in the dress are indentured apprentices of this works, bound for seven years to the trade of bell-founder and moulder, and their indentures are lodged with this claim. By those articles they are to serve faithfully, to keep the master's secrets, and to do no damage to his goods; the master for his part is to teach the mystery of the trade, to find them meat, drink and lodging, and to pay the wage set out. Our discipline is written in the same paper and is not a dead letter. Absence without leave, sixpence; drunkenness in the works, one shilling and a caution; a third offence, the indenture at hazard. Gates shut at six. No boy handles the bell-metal at the melt in his first two years, that being twenty parts of tin in the hundred, brittle as glass when cold and unforgiving when hot. It is a hard schooling. But we have not lost a lad to the furnace in nineteen years, and we would rather fine a boy a shilling than bury him.

CUSTOMS ENTRY. Coasting entry inwards, No. 218, 1862. Consignee: the Commissioners' store, for the Skerryvore ground. Shipper: Caldwell Brothers, Falkirk. Goods: finished bronze castings, bell-metal of 20 per cent tin, delivered under contract and entered from the delivery ledger produced with this entry. Ledger particulars, examined and found to agree with the packages landed: Folio 41. Two bells, 3 cwt 2 qr and 1 cwt 3 qr 7 lb., each turned, tuned and marked with the founders' name and the year. Folio 42. Six bearing bushes, together 2 cwt 0 qr 21 lb., bored to gauge. Folio 43. Twelve fog-bell hammers with their springs, 1 cwt 1 qr. Folio 44. Four valve seatings, 3 qr 12 lb., rough from the sand and to be finished here. Folio 45. One spare casting, weight not entered in the ledger; weighed on the King's beam at 2 qr 4 lb. and so entered by me. Total weight landed, 9 cwt 3 qr 16 lb. against 9 cwt 3 qr 12 lb. in the ledger; the difference of 4 lb. lies within the beam's error and the brackish sediment adhering to the two bushes stowed lowest, which were not cleaned before weighing. All packages opened and compared with the ledger folios. Nothing short, nothing broken. Duty not chargeable, the goods being of home manufacture and coastwise. Entry passed.

Caldwell Brothers, Falkirk. Delivery book, 1877. Folio 19. May 2. Delivered to Carswell and Co., Glasgow: two bells, bell-metal, twenty parts tin, finished and tuned, 1 cwt 3 qr and 2 cwt 1 qr. Carted to the canal basin. Signed for by their man Wishart, who signed without reading, as he always does. May 4. Delivered to the Trustees at Kilbrannan Sound: one fog bell, alloy as above, 3 cwt, with yoke, staple and clapper complete. Sent by the Ardrossan boat. Note: this is the third bell to that quarter in two years and I should dearly like to know what becomes of them. May 9. Delivered to J. Hetherington, ironmonger: six small castings, sundry, per his order of the 2nd. Weight 41 lb. Paid on delivery, which I record with feeling. May 11. The two bells returned by Carswell, unpaid for, on the complaint that the note is flat. The note is not flat. The note is exactly what he ordered, and he ordered wrong. Mr. Andrew has gone through to argue it and will lose, being too polite for the work. May 16. Delivered to the same Trustees: one spare clapper, 11 lb. May 21. Recast the Carswell pair, same alloy, half a hundredweight lighter, and delivered again. Charge for remelting entered fol. 20. He took them and said nothing of the first lot, which is as near an apology as that house has ever produced. Carried forward.

Survey report. Caldwell Brothers, Falkirk. Damage by fire at the works, 3rd January 1861. Survey made the 7th and 8th. The fire broke out in the pattern loft at or about eleven at night and was got under by four in the morning. The cause is not determined. The watchman states that the stove in the loft was drawn at eight. Damages found as follows. Pattern loft: roof burnt off, floor fallen in. The stock of wooden patterns is a total loss, some eleven hundred pieces by the works list. This is the heaviest item and cannot be made good by purchase. Moulding shop: roof timbers charred, slates broken, sand floor fouled with fallen debris. Two crane legs distorted by heat and to be renewed. Furnace house: little affected. The bell-metal in stock, twenty parts tin in the hundred, lay in the store and is recovered, though the pigs are scaled and must be reweighed before use. Timber store: a quantity of oak, part of it waterlogged and lying under water in the tank, is undamaged, the tank having checked the fire on that side. Office: books and drawings saved, being carried out by the clerk. Estimate of the whole damage, exclusive of the patterns, 940 pounds. The patterns are valued by the firm at 1600 pounds. That figure is not accepted without further evidence of the stock held. Work suspended in the moulding shop for six weeks.

CALDWELL BROTHERS, FALKIRK. -- Foundry ledger, 1865. Folio 47, account of bell-metal work. May 11. -- To one bell, of the house bell-metal, twenty parts of tin in the hundred, weight 2 cwt. 3 qrs. 18 lb., cast and tuned to order for the harbour trustees, and forwarded by rail and thence by the packet. June 2. -- By the said bell returned upon our hands, carriage forward, and the charge accordingly suspended. Note of the complaint. -- The trustees' clerk writes from the shore of Kilbrannan Sound that upon being hung and struck the bell gave a note at once flat and short, dying almost as soon as sounded, and that a flaw could be traced with the finger nail for four inches upward from the lip; he observes further that the crown is thicker upon one side than the other, so that the bell hangs untrue. Examined here in the presence of both partners. The flaw is a cold shut and not a crack, the metal having been poured too slowly and the mould insufficiently vented; the thickness is confirmed, the core having lifted. The mixture itself is not at fault, being of the full twenty per cent. of tin and of good clean ring in the sample bar retained. Ordered: the bell to be broken and remelted, the metal carried to stock at its value; a second to be cast in the coming month, with the mould vented afresh; no charge to the trustees for the recasting, and the carriage both ways to be borne by us.

LABORATORY NOTE. 1872. Sample 17. Origin: casting broken out of a concretion, Gantock shoal. Foundry mark, Penrose and Gill, Truro. Description: sand-cast bronze, leaded. Moulding sand impressed on the reverse face. Weight 6 lb 4 oz. Assay: copper the bulk; tin about 6 parts in the hundred; lead present in quantity, shown in the fracture as fine grey specks throughout. Colour: reddish, distinctly darker than the yellow of the high-tin metals. Grain: open rather than close. Fracture rough, crystal visible to the naked eye at the thicker part. Hardness: a smooth file cuts freely. The metal takes a burr under the graver. On percussion: hung on twine and struck with a light hammer, the casting gives a short dull note, damped almost at once. Sound dies within two seconds. No ring worth the name. Remark: the lead accounts for it. Such metal works kindly at the bench and wears well in a bearing, but it is not bell-stuff and was never meant for it. Filed.

INSURANCE ASSESSMENT. 2nd August 1866. Machrihanish bay. In the matter of a consignment of leaded bronze, six parts tin in the hundred, cast and invoiced by Penrose and Gill, Truro. The undersigned, having been appointed to report upon the difference between the assured and the said founders, finds as follows: (a) The invoice of the aforementioned foundry charges nine hundredweight three quarters at the rate of one hundred and twelve pounds the ton, together with pattern money. (b) The assured, upon landing, weighed the goods at nine hundredweight one quarter and fourteen pounds, and objects further that the rate exceeds the quotation given by letter in April last by four pounds the ton. (c) Part of the consignment was landed in concretion from the beach and had to be cleaned before weighing, whereby some small allowance may be due to the said founders. (d) No damage is alleged such as would fall upon the policy, the whole difference being one of weight and price between buyer and seller. The undersigned accordingly recommends that the claim be declined as outside the risk, without prejudice to the assured's remedy against Penrose and Gill in the ordinary course.

HARBOUR MASTER'S LOG. The Gantock shoal station. 27th May 1864. Wind SW, moderate, hazy. Tides ordinary. Nothing to report of the shoal, the beacon standing well. Attended the weighbridge at ten o'clock upon the dispute between Messrs Penrose and Gill of Truro and the consignees, touching the consignment of leaded bronze landed here on the 24th. The founders' invoice states four tons twelve hundredweight of their leaded bronze, six parts of tin in the hundred, at the price agreed per ton. The consignees weighed it upon landing at four tons seven, and refuse the difference, alleging further that a leaded metal is not worth the price of a true gunmetal and that the invoice is dear by two pounds the ton. I caused the whole to be weighed again in my presence, the bridge having been proved this spring. Result: four tons nine hundredweight and two quarters, the balance being, I judge, in the dunnage and the wet sand still clinging to the castings, which no man should be asked to pay for as bronze. Certified accordingly. As to the price, that is between the parties and their lawyers, and I told them so. The tide would not wait upon their arithmetic, and neither would I.

SURVEY REPORT upon castings delivered, made at Machrihanish bay, 1867, the goods being from Penrose and Gill of Truro and of leaded bronze at 6 per cent tin as specified. I was directed to compare the goods against the delivery ledger and to certify the same. Method: each package opened, the contents counted, weighed on the harbour beam, and measured at two diameters at right angles with the callipers. Ledger, and my findings against it: Entry 96, eight pump liners, ledger 4 cwt 1 qr; found 4 cwt 1 qr 3 lb.; bores between 5.98 and 6.03 inches, tolerance allowed 0.05. Entry 97, twenty-four gland rings, ledger 1 cwt 2 qr; found the same; all within gauge. Entry 98, three stern bushes, ledger 6 cwt exactly; found 5 cwt 3 qr 20 lb. One bush shows a cold shut on the flange, 2 inches long, not through the metal. Entry 99, forty bolts and nuts, counted 39. One deficient. Entry 100, one spare liner, not weighed at the works, here 0 cwt 2 qr 8 lb. Totals: ledger 12 cwt 0 qr 8 lb.; landed 11 cwt 3 qr 27 lb. I certify the delivery substantially in accordance with the ledger, subject to the missing bolt at entry 99 and to the flaw noted at entry 98, both of which I have reported to the founders. The concretion upon three liners is from the quay and not from the metal.

Harbour master's log, Sanda roads. 3rd September 1876. Wind sou'west, fresh; raining since Tuesday. Two smacks in for shelter, nothing landed, nothing owing. I copy the pattern-maker's account into this book because the office at Campbeltown lost the last one I sent and then contrived to imply I had never sent it. Account of Mr. Silas Trenoweth, pattern-maker, for work to the order of Penrose and Gill, Truro, in the matter of our new mooring fittings, the castings to be leaded bronze of six parts tin as specified: To one pattern for a mooring ring, in yellow pine, with core box - 1 pound 6s. To two patterns for bollard caps, ditto, with prints and fillets - 2 pounds 2s. To dressing and varnishing the same - 7s 6d. To alterations following Penrose's letter of the 11th, the draught being too little for the sand and the moulder unable to lift the pattern clean - 14s. To carriage, Truro to the works - 3s 4d. Total - 4 pounds 12s 10d. I add, for the record, that the alterations were no fault of Trenoweth's. He built to the drawing he was given, and the drawing was made by a gentleman who has never in his life pulled a pattern out of a mould. Trenoweth said as much, mildly, in a letter I have kept by me. Castings expected before Martinmas. If they are late I shall be moored to the same rotten ring another winter, and I shall have opinions about it.

Harbour Master's Log, Kilbrannan Sound. Entry of the 12th November, 1864. BE IT RECORDED that there was this day brought into the office by the boatmen of the station one casting of bronze, the same having been drawn from the ground in a mass of concretion, and the said concretion in part struck away before delivery. AND IT IS FURTHER RECORDED that the said casting bears the mark of the Marrable Foundry of Whitby, and is by the certificate of that house a gunmetal of about eleven parts of tin in the hundred parts, cast in sand. AND WHEREAS the crust being removed from one quarter the metal was exposed, the same is found of a reddish yellow colour, and the grain thereof open and coarse rather than close, as appears upon the broken lug. AND the same being struck with the office hammer, it returned a note dull and short, without continuance or sweetness, such as is proper to a metal of this proportion and not to be taken as any defect therein. Entered by me, and the article laid aside in the west shed pending instruction.

MANIFEST of goods shipped in good order aboard the coasting smack Jessie, at the port of Stranraer, this 16th day of April 1863, to be delivered at Whitby, freight as agreed. MARK. -- M.F.W., in a diamond. 1. One case, said to contain one gunmetal valve body, of the mixture of eleven parts of tin in the hundred, weight declared 3 cwt. 1 qr. 7 lb., being the piece delivered by the Marrable Foundry, Whitby, in February last, and now RETURNED TO THE MAKERS AS FLAWED, the shippers declining to accept the same. Shipper's remark, entered at his desire. -- The casting was found, upon being opened out in the dry store at Loch Ryan and set up for fitting, to carry a run of blowholes along the upper flange and a scab at the boss, so that it would not face true and could not be made tight at any pressure; the ring of it, moreover, was dull. The shippers have to observe, with all courtesy to the foundry, whose work has hitherto given them satisfaction, that the fault is one of moulding and not of carriage, the case having come to hand sound and the straw undisturbed, and they look for a sound piece in exchange, or the price returned, at the makers' election. 2. Two casks, empty, returned. 3. One bundle, patterns, on loan, to be given up with the foregoing. Freight and primage as per bill of lading. Signed for the master, D. TROTTER.

Report of survey, Marrable Foundry, Whitby, 1867. Sanda roads district. On the apprentices and the discipline of the works. Seven boys are bound here by indenture, none under thirteen years. The indentures were produced to me and read over. The terms are seven years. The boy is bound to serve his master faithfully, to keep his secrets, to do no damage, not to haunt taverns nor play at cards or dice, and not to absent himself by day or night without leave. The master for his part binds himself to teach the art and mystery of moulding and founding, to find the boy in working clothes and aprons, and to pay wages rising from three shillings in the first year to eleven in the last. Discipline: hours are six to six with an hour at noon. The gate is shut on the stroke and a fine of twopence taken for lateness. A fine book is kept and I saw it. Two boys fined this quarter, one for leaving the shop in work hours, one for spoiling a mould in horseplay at the sand heap. The boys are set first to riddling and carrying sand, then to ramming, and are not allowed at the pouring until the fourth year. The house metal is gunmetal at eleven of tin, and the mixture is taught to them by weight on the scale, never by eye, which I commend. Premises orderly, floor sanded, ladles in good order. I find the indentures regular and the discipline reasonable.

MARRABLE FOUNDRY, WHITBY. Ledger of Indentures and Works Discipline. Folio 41. Year 1871. Whereas Josiah Peart, aged fifteen years, is this day bound apprentice to the said foundry for the term of seven years, the covenants are entered as follows: 1. That the said apprentice shall serve diligently in the moulding shop, and shall be instructed in the mixing and pouring of gunmetal of eleven parts tin in the hundred, and in such other work as the master shall direct. 2. That he shall not absent himself, nor frequent taverns, nor disclose the proportions of the said mixtures to any person not of the works. 3. Wages: two shillings weekly in the first year, rising by sixpence yearly thereafter. DISCIPLINE, entered against the same folio: 12th May. Apprentice Peart fined sixpence, being late at the gate three mornings. 3rd July. Apprentice Peart cautioned for spoiling a mould, no fine, the fault being partly that of the journeyman. 19th September. Fined one shilling for tampering with the crucible tongs whilst metal was down. The master notes that a further offence of the like kind shall be reported to the aforementioned boy's father and to the magistrates.

DIVE LOG. Ardmore approaches. 8th June 1869. Slack water at 11.40. Two descents, seven fathoms, bottom foul. Little visibility on the ebb. Note entered here for the record, the question having been raised on the boat as to who may be sent down. Our lads are indentured apprentices of the Marrable Foundry, Whitby, bound to the founder's trade, and their articles say nothing of the diving dress; they were lent to this work by the master's leave and at his charge. By the indenture they serve five years, keep the works' hours, and are taught the melting and moulding of the house metal, a gunmetal of eleven parts of tin. They are not to frequent taverns, not to absent themselves, and not to hire themselves elsewhere without leave, which last is the clause that concerns us here. Discipline at the works is strict and, to my mind, sensible. Fines are read out on Saturdays. A boy is kept from the crucible until his third year. I have written to the master that a lad who may not be trusted with hot metal at nineteen ought not to be sent into ten fathoms of cold water at seventeen, and that if the practice continues I will not take them in my boat. Second descent abandoned, tide making.

NOTICE. To the Editor of the Ayr Advertiser. Sir, - I am foreman moulder at the Dunlivet Works, Ayr, and I put this in your paper to save argument, for I have been asked the same question a dozen times since the Kilbrannan Sound business. Our work is a leaded bronze, sand-cast, about seven parts of tin in the hundred, with the lead put in to make it kind under the tool. I make no secret of it. It is an honest metal for glands, bushes and bearings, and I will stand by it against any works in the west of Scotland. But I will not have it called bell-metal, and I will not have men sell it as such. Break a piece across and look at it. The grain is coarser than the high-tin work, open in patches where the lead lies in it, and the colour of the fracture is a dull reddish yellow, not the pale grey you get off a bell-metal. Strike it and you hear the difference at once. It gives a short dull note, more of a thud than a ring, and it dies away directly your hand comes near it. The castings now lying in our dry store may be seen and struck by any man who doubts me. - I am, Sir, yours, W. Tarbet.

Report of survey: the beacon fittings, Ardmore approaches. February 1861. To the Commissioners. Gentlemen, I went over the ground on the 9th, in weather that does not encourage lingering, and I have since been through the works at Dunlivet, Ayr, who are to supply the new fittings in leaded bronze of seven parts tin. With the metal I have no quarrel. It pours easily, takes a clean skin, and will stand the wet on that shore better than any iron you have yet put there. My quarrel is with the pattern-maker's account, which I attach, and which the Commissioners will find heavier than they expect: To patterns for two lantern brackets, mahogany, with core boxes - 3 pounds 15s. To one pattern for the base flange, yellow pine - 1 pound 8s. To recutting the flange pattern, the first having warped in the drying - 12s. To wax fillets, prints and varnish - 9s 6d. To carriage - 4s. Total - 6 pounds 8s 6d. Six pounds odd for wooden shapes that will never go to sea strikes a committee as extravagance. It is nothing of the kind. The pattern is the whole of the job; the mould is only sand agreeing with it for an afternoon. Pay the account, and pay it without the customary three letters of protest, and you will have castings that fit the first time they are offered up. I recommend that the order proceed without alteration. A. Menteith, surveyor.

NOTICE. To the Editor. Sir, permit me to place before the trade the facts of a dispute now pending. On the 4th of March last the Dunlivet Works, Ayr, despatched to my order a consignment of leaded bronze castings, seven parts tin in the hundred, for shipwork. The consignment was invoiced at four tons three hundredweight and charged at the rate agreed, with an addition for the lead. The goods were landed at the Tarbert narrows and weighed at the public beam before two witnesses. The weight returned was three tons seventeen hundredweight, being six hundredweight short of the invoice. The foundry contends that the difference is accounted for by the crates and the packing sand, these being included in their own weighing at the works. This is denied. The crates were weighed empty at the beam and are entered at two hundredweight one quarter. The foundry declines to abate the price and has rendered an account for the whole. There is besides a question upon the rate, the invoice charging at the gunmetal figure and not at the figure quoted to me in writing for leaded metal. The matter is referred to arbitration, a referee having been named by the parties. Until it is determined the account is held unpaid. I am, Sir, your obedient servant, A MERCHANT OF THE NARROWS.

DIVE LOG kept by the diver in the employ of the Dunlivet Works, Ayr. 1869. Tuesday, 25th May. -- Down twice in Kilbrannan Sound upon the sunk lighter, forty minutes and thirty-five, bottom hard with concretion; nothing got up but one length of chain. Water very thick after noon; came up and the pumps were housed. Wednesday, 26th May. -- No diving, wind fresh at south-west. Being ashore and idle, I was desired by Mr. Semple to go over to the coal ree and take account of the coke landed for the works, the foreman being from home; and I set down what I found, that it may not be lost. Of the coke delivered by the last two cargoes, some eleven tons remain in the shed and about four in the open, and the last is the worse for the rain, being slacked and dirty and full of small. Mr. Semple's word to me was that the cupola will not do its work upon wet coke, that the melt comes sluggish and the metal dull, and that he had rather have ten tons dry than twenty wet. I have to note further that the Ayr merchant's coke burns short and leaves much ash, and that the works' leaded bronze, seven parts of tin in the hundred with the lead besides, is reckoned by him to want a steady quick fire above all things. Recommended that the shed be extended before the winter and the open stack tarpaulined. Thursday, 27th May. -- Down once, twenty minutes. Log continued overleaf.

Deposition of Angus Rae, furnaceman at the Dunlivet Works, Ayr, taken at Machrihanish bay, 1868. I have charge of the fires and the fuel, and I am asked what we burn and where it comes from. We burn coke under the pots and nothing else. It comes by the Ayr boats in sacks, two ton at a delivery, and is stacked under the lean to at the west gable, off the ground on boards, because coke that has lain wet is worth little. Good coke is hard and grey, it rings in the sack when you shift it, and it breaks bright. The soft slack sort smokes, throws no heat into the pot, and leaves the bars fouled. Since March we have been served short and served badly, with a wet dusty coke that clinkers on the bars and wants raking twice in a melt. It costs us near an hour on every heat. That is a serious matter with our own metal, which is a leaded bronze at seven of tin. Hold it long and hot on a poor fire and the lead sweats out of it and the metal drinks up gas, and then the casting comes spongy and the fault is laid at my door. There was talk of drying peat and burning that under the pots, as they do at some inland places. I have tried peat in the smith's fire only. It will not answer for melting. It is a soft slow heat and a dirty one. I said so to the manager and he was of the same mind. That is the whole of what I know of the fuel.

Sanda roads, 14th November 1870. My dear Sir, In answer to yours, and speaking as one who will not be held to more than he says, the matter of the sulphur in old oak stands thus. First, that timber which has lain long under water and out of the air takes up sulphur into its substance, the same being formed in the black mud about it, where the water is foul and without air, and being carried in with the iron of the fastenings. Second, that whilst the said timber remains wet, no harm appears, and the piece may be handled and looks sound enough. Third, that upon drying in the open air the sulphur aforementioned takes up air and turns to an acid, being of the nature of oil of vitriol, whereupon the wood weeps, salts break out white and yellow upon the face of it, and the substance grows brittle and falls to powder at the edges. I have seen this in staves lifted here, and in a knee that stood two winters in a shed and is now no better than tinder. Concretion upon the surface does not save it; if anything it holds the mischief in. My counsel, therefore, is to keep such oak wet until you can wash the sulphur out of it, and not to dry it for the pleasure of seeing it. I remain, yours faithfully.

CLAIM FOR SALVAGE AND FOR ALLOWANCE OF LOSS. Loch Ryan, 1865. It is with some reluctance, and only because the underwriters have pressed for an accounting of the condition of the timber landed, that I set down at length what every man who has drawn oak out of a brackish bottom already knows: namely, that wherever an iron bolt, spike, or knee has lain in contact with the wood, the wood about it is gone soft and black for a hand's breadth on every side, whilst timber a foot away from any iron remains sound enough to be worked with the adze. The sediment of the loch is brackish and foul, and the iron in it rusts and stains; and the stain does not merely colour the wood but works upon its very substance, the cellulose being wasted and eaten away far faster in the neighbourhood of the iron than elsewhere, as though the metal hastened a decay which it does not itself suffer and is not consumed in hastening. Of nineteen futtocks raised, eleven are condemned; and every one of the eleven was bolted. I claim accordingly.

Assessment upon the timbers recovered at Machrihanish bay. My dear sir, - you will forgive me for writing this out as a letter instead of upon the printed form, but the printed form has no line for the one thing that signifies, and I would rather be irregular than useless. The timbers came out of brackish sediment and they are waterlogged through and through. They look sound. They are not sound. The wood substance is largely gone out of them and what holds the shape is the water in the cells, nothing else. Let that water away and the shape goes with it: the piece shrinks, checks, splits along the rays and curls like a shaving, and no treatment afterwards will bring it back. I have seen it done at Ayr with a stern knee that was perfect when landed and firewood in a fortnight, and the yard could not understand it. So: keep them wet. Immersed, not damped. Under water in a tank or a lined pit, sacking over, out of the sun, and topped up. Keep them so until the treatment is arranged and the man is engaged to do it, however long that takes. I have valued them as recoverable on that condition only. Yours, etc.

The Gantock shoal, 1864. My dear Hargreaves, You will forgive the form of this. I am a lawyer before I am a correspondent, and I set the matter out as I should set out a case. First, that bronze lying in seawater does not waste evenly, as iron wastes, but loses one of its metals in preference to the other. Second, that it is the zinc and the tin which go, being the baser, and the copper which is left behind. Third, and here is the point of my letter, that the casting keeps its shape and very nearly its dimensions to the eye, and yet is left with a soft copper-rich skin, dull salmon in colour, which may be pared away with a pocket knife. Fourth, that beneath the said skin the sound metal may be greatly reduced, so that a fitting which measures true upon the rule will fail under any load whatever. I pared such a skin this day from a cock taken out of the brackish sediment on the shoal, a full eighth of an inch of it, red as a new penny and of no more strength than putty. Have a care, therefore, before you certify such work sound upon its appearance merely. Yours in haste, E. Muir.

Salvage claim. Tarbert narrows, 1877. Made by me, Thomas Gair, diver. I am asking for extra time and extra hands, and here is the reason. The metal we are after is not lying bare on the bottom. Every piece of it is grown over. First the weed and the small shell take hold, then the worm-tubes and the acorn shells build on top of them, then the sand and the broken shell get caught in among the lot, and the whole business sets up as hard as a paving stone. On the big casting the crust runs a good inch and a half thick. You cannot brush it off. You cannot get a hand under it. I had to go at it with a chisel and a mallet under water, and a chisel under water is slow work. When it does come away it comes in plates, and the metal beneath is clean, so there is no harm to the goods. Two days on the one piece. I ask for that time. Landed and held in dry store at the shed until the survey. Th. Gair, his hand.

Laboratory note, the Ardmore approaches, 1866. There is a black band a foot beneath the surface of the estuary mud that will teach a chemist more in one afternoon than a week among his books. Turn a spade of it and the thing announces itself before ever you reach the bench: that smell of rotten eggs, sulphuretted hydrogen, coming up out of the ooze in slow bubbles. The reason is plain enough once seen. Down there the air cannot get in. The water in the pores is stagnant, the oxygen is spent by the decay of weed and creature, and something must still carry off the corruption. What is left is the sulphate that every gallon of seawater carries in abundance, and it is that which is drawn down, robbed of its oxygen, and delivered up as sulphide. Hence the blackness, which is iron sulphide, and hence the stink. The same business goes forward in my stoppered jar of seawater on the shelf, left standing since spring with a little weed in it: black at the bottom, foul at the neck, the very same chemistry playing itself out in a different vessel and a different matter. Bottom mud or bottled water, shut the air away and the sulphur goes the same road.

CUSTOMS ENTRY. The Ardmore approaches. 1874. Goods entered: oak timbers, nine pieces, taken up out of peat and now lying in the dry store. Duty: nil, no merchantable value assigned. Remarks of the entering officer, set down at more length than the book requires, my wife's brother being a joiner and forever asking me about such stuff. Peat keeps wood. That is the whole of it, and a strange thing it is to handle. There is no air down in the peat, and the water in it is sour, so the worm will not live there and the rot cannot take hold. A piece of oak may lie in it a hundred years and better and come up whole, with the adze marks on it as fresh as the day they were struck, and the pegs still in their holes. It comes up near black, the peat water having stained it clean through. It is heavy as stone with the water it has taken up, and yet soft as cheese under the thumb for all that it looks sound, and I would not trust a hundredweight upon any of it. Entered nil accordingly. - J. Pentreath, Officer.

CUSTOMS ENTRY. Port book, 1862. Entered inwards from the Ardmore approaches: one lot recovered ironwork, 3 cwt 1 qr; two casks of peat and mud brought up with it, 40 gallons. Officer's remark, made as the casks were opened for examination: The mud is black peat mud from below the surface layer, the surface being some three inches of brown ooze and the black stuff beneath it. On being disturbed it gives off a strong smell of sulphuretted hydrogen, as of rotten eggs, very sharp at the first opening and still perceptible at eight feet from the cask after a quarter of an hour. The diver reports the same upon the bottom: that the water is sweet enough until his boots go in, and that the moment he stirs the mud the stink rises into his helmet and stays with him the whole of the dive, forty minutes on this occasion. Casks stoppered and set outside the shed by my direction. Goods passed. Duty nil, being wreck. J. Ferrier, Officer.

LEDGER OF THE WORKS. Folio 41. 1865. Nov. 14. To carriage of castings shipped for Kilbrannan Sound, per master's account rendered. Sum entered. Memorandum, taken from the master's letter of the same date and copied here for the account. No sight of sun or star these two days. Thick overhead throughout. Position by dead reckoning only. Course by compass, corrected for variation and for the deviation card. Distance by log, hove each hour and entered on the slate. Leeway allowed by eye from the wake; set of tide allowed from the tables, not observed. Reckoning carried forward from the last observed position, that of the 9th, noon. Note: error is to be presumed in such a reckoning, and to grow with every hour run from the last sight. The master states as much himself. Goods therefore to be held to this account as at date of shipment, and not as at the position reported. Entered by the clerk. Checked.

SURVEY REPORT. Loch Ryan. Running survey of the ground between Cairnryan and the Scar. 1867. Method. Boat under oars. Two hands at the lead, one at the book. Angles taken by sextant to three fixed marks at each cast, times noted by watch, soundings reduced to low water spring tides. Lead. Deep-sea lead, 28 lb, armed with tallow in the hollow at every cast. Finding of a hard bottom. Over soft ground the lead beds itself, the line goes slack in the hand, and the tallow brings up mud, ooze or peat. Over hard ground the lead brings up nothing, or a chip of stone only, and the blow is felt through the line at once, short and dry. The arming is then clean, or bruised and bright where it has taken the rock. Result. A hard patch found bearing S.W. by W. from the Scar, 4 3/4 fathoms at low water, the casts on either hand giving 9 and 11 fathoms in soft ground. Arming clean on nine casts out of eleven upon the patch. Remarks. The patch is small and was run over twice before it was struck, the tracks lying too wide apart for such ground. Waterlogged oak taken up on its eastern edge. A close survey is recommended before the ground is used.

My dear Hallam, You send me a position as though you were sending me a street and a door number, and I must tell you what it is you have actually sent. The place given for the loss on the Skerryvore ground was got by dead reckoning at the end of a foul night, by men who had been eleven hours without sight of sun or star, in a boat driven they knew not how far. Call the error five miles, and I am being kind. You have not given me a point at all. You have given me a circle five miles about, and that circle is nearer eighty square miles of open water. Eighty square miles! Consider what that is. Our sweep covers a lane perhaps a hundred yards broad, and we make good, in a fair day, some twelve miles of lane. Reckon it out and you will find you are asking for a summer's work, and paying for it, to cover the ground once over. Send me a bearing off the light, or send me a man who took a sounding, and I will halve your circle. Send me nothing, and I shall send you the bill. Yours ever, R. C.

NOTICE. - To Owners and to Gentlemen Employing Sounding Boats. I have been these twenty years working the lead in Kilbrannan Sound, and as I am asked the same question by every party that engages me, I will answer it here in print and be done with it. What the lead tells you over a wreck depends altogether on how the wreck lies. Take a long one, a vessel stretched out on the ground with her length along the bottom. You will get your shoaling by degrees. The lead comes up a fathom short, then two, and it holds shoal cast after cast for a cable's length or more before it deepens away again. You cannot miss such a thing if you run your lines across her at any reasonable spacing, and you get her length and her lie into the bargain. Now take a small compact one, a boiler, an engine, a heap of iron in a lump. One cast is short and the next is right again, and if your boat is a few yards to one side you have nothing at all. I have run over such a mark a dozen times and touched it twice. Space your lines close, and run them twice, crossways. That is my whole advice. JOHN M'ILWRAITH, sounding-man.

CUSTOMS ENTRY. The Gantock shoal. 1874. Entry No. 318. Article: one fitting, bronze or brass, recovered from the shoal, encased in concretion. Particulars recorded in the order the Board requires: 1. Gross weight as landed, with the concretion upon it, 63 lb 8 oz. Net weight after dressing, 41 lb 2 oz. 2. Extreme dimensions over the concretion, 19 1/2 in. by 8 in. by 7 1/4 in. 3. Character of the concretion: hard, grey, shelly, closely adhering, thickness from 3/8 in. to 1 1/4 in. 4. Marks, numbers or founder's name: none legible before dressing. To be re-entered when read. 5. Place and depth of recovery: 6 fathoms, bearings entered in the margin. 6. Date landed; name of the salvor; vessel by which brought in. 7. Value declared: 3l., as metal only. Note for officers. The entry ought to record the weight both before and after dressing, and the marks as read off the metal, with the bearings. Wanting these, the article cannot afterwards be identified with any certainty, and the entry is of no use to anybody.

SALVAGE CLAIM. Schedule C. Gantock shoal, 1877. Charge for the keeping of recovered timber. Item. One tank, iron, built in the yard for this service. Length 22 feet, breadth 6 feet, depth 4 feet. Item. Tank filled with water to cover, the timber lying wholly submerged. No part left standing in air. Ground of the charge: timber raised from the bottom is soaked through. Laid out in the open it dries at the surface, splits from end to end, and shrinks away from its fastenings within the week. Two futtocks were so lost on the second day, before the tank was ready. Item. Water drawn off foul and changed weekly. Nine changes to date. Item. Boards and pig-iron laid on top to hold the pieces down, the timber being buoyant once the concretion is knocked off. Item. Watchman nightly, the tank standing in the open yard. Charge submitted for the tank, the labour, and the keeping, ninety days. Surveyor's note: the arrangement is proper and the charge is allowed.

Sir, - Touching the object lately raised in Kilbrannan Sound and now lying in your keeping, I beg leave to set down my opinion in form, that there may be no mistaking it hereafter. FIRST, that the object is at present wholly enclosed in a crust of concretion, and that the crust is not dirt but the case which now holds the article together. SECONDLY, that no part of the said crust be broken, chipped, or picked away until the object shall have been examined and a record made of it as it stands, since what is struck off cannot be restored. THIRDLY, that from the moment of lifting the object be kept immersed, first in seawater and thereafter in fresh water frequently renewed, and never suffered to dry, whether in whole or in part. FOURTHLY, that the salts within be drawn out by such washing over a term of weeks before any attempt is made upon the crust. FIFTHLY, that when the crust is at length removed, the same be done under water and with hand tools only. I hold every one of these to be needful, and the second the most needful of all. Your obedient servant.

Harbour Master's Log. The Skerryvore ground. 1870. I write this in my own hand and I want it kept in the book, for it has now happened three times and I will not have it said I gave no warning. The oak that comes up off the ground is full of water right through, and it is not the sound timber it looks. Lay it out in the open untreated and it dries from the outside inward. The outside shrinks and the inside does not, and the wood tears itself apart. The knees landed on Tuesday were whole when they came out of the boat. By Friday they had checked along the grain from end to end, and one has opened a split I can lay three fingers in. A rib went to a bundle of splinters inside the week and could not be lifted whole off the stones. Nothing whatever was done to them. They were laid on the quay in the sun and the wind, which I now see is the worst usage they could have had. I have ordered the remainder kept under seawater in the trough until some man who knows the business tells me otherwise. - R. Dunn, Harbour Master.

Harbour Master's Log. Ardmore approaches. 1876. Being asked by the Trustees to state why the wreck in the approaches is worth less to us every season that we leave her lying, I record here what the divers report and what I have seen for myself of the pieces landed. Whatever timber stands proud of the mud is eaten. The shipworm gets into it end-on and burrows away down the grain, so that a frame which appears sound and even handsome on the outside is found, when it is sawn across, to be a mere honeycomb of chalky tubes that will not bear its own weight out of water; and the gribble, working from the surface inward, planes away the outside in a fine fretted rot until the timber wastes like a candle. But the same frame, where it lies buried in the mud, is hard and sweet and takes a nail; and the line between the two conditions is as plain upon the wood as a tide mark upon a pier. The lesson is that what we do not raise soon, above the mud, we shall not raise at all. Entered this day.

Deposition of the diver, taken at Loch Ryan, 1874. Being asked how I tell a ballast mound from a hull when I am down and can see the length of my arm and no further, I say this, and I say it as I would to any man in the trade. A ballast mound lies like stones lie. It is a heap. Long and low, higher in the middle, and the sides spilled out where they gave way when the wood went from under. Every stone is loose. You take one off and there is another beneath it, and it is round beach stone or quarry rubble, not shaped for anything. Round the foot of it the ground is clean. That is your whole story: the ship is gone and only her ballast is left, lying in the shape of the hold that held it. A hull is a shape, and you know it in a minute. You feel the frames come up under the hand at even spacing, and the planking across them, and it runs fair in a line and curves the way a vessel curves. The oak is waterlogged soft, so soft you may push a knife in to the hilt, but it is still timber and still fastened. Stones in a heap: ballast. Timber in a curve: hull. There is no mistaking one for the other with the hand on it.

INSURANCE ASSESSMENT. Sanda roads. 1878. Whereas the assured contends that the obstruction struck was not marked upon the chart, and whereas the underwriters contend that it was sufficiently marked, the assessor recites as follows: That the chart in use is founded upon a survey of 1841, described upon its own face as a running survey, and bearing the caution that the soundings are not to be relied upon between the tracks; That an obstruction of unknown character and unknown depth is there shown by the abbreviation Obstn., without name and without figure of depth; That a wreck whose position is doubtful is shown by the letters P.D. set against it, and one merely reported by the letters P.A., neither being evidence of position; That a rock awash at low water is shown by a cross, and a rock whose very existence is doubtful by a cross within a dotted circle; That the mark relied upon by the assured is an Obstn. with P.D. against it, lying in a part of these roads where the survey tracks are upwards of a mile apart. The assessor finds that the chart gave warning that something lay thereabouts, and gave no warning whatever as to where it lay. Liability is not excluded upon this ground. Sum reserved pending survey.

Salvage claim, Gantock shoal, 1865. Statement of how the ground was covered, in support of the days charged. I had no marks to work from, being out of sight of anything but the light, so I did it by compass and by watch, and I did it the same way every day. We took a course north by east, held it steady, and ran twenty minutes by the watch at half speed, which I call four cables to the minute with that tide, and I noted the time in and the time out in the book. Then round on to the reverse course, offset a hundred yards by the log line streamed astern, and run the twenty minutes back. So on, up and down, like ploughing a field. The book shows every leg, the course steered, the time started, the time stopped. Twenty-two lanes on the first ground, nineteen on the second. Any man can lay it out on the chart from my book and see that we missed nothing wider than a hundred yards. That is the work I am charging for. J. Ross, master of the smack Ivy.

My dear Robert, - You ask how it comes about that the wreck is not where the mate solemnly swears he left her, and since you ask I shall give you the whole of it with the relish it deserves. Picture the man. Thick weather in the Ardmore approaches, no land, no sight, the vessel going down under him, and he does the one creditable thing left: he pulls out his watch, notes the hour, and works his position from the noon before. He writes it down. He believes it. He will swear to it in any court in the kingdom, and he will be honestly and completely wrong. For all the while he was running his hours, the flood was carrying the whole sea he floated in bodily to the north-east at better than two knots, and it carried him with it as a river carries a leaf, without his feeling the least motion. The log measures her passage through the water. It knows nothing whatever of where the water itself has gone. Six hours of that and you are three miles from your paper position and perfectly certain of your arithmetic. So they drag where he says, and find sand, and call him a liar. He is nothing of the sort. He is a man who reckoned in a moving room. Search a wide box, and search it down-tide. Ever yours.

Laboratory note, entered as a letter to Dr. Yuille, it being easier to write it so. My dear Yuille, - the dress off the Kilbrannan Sound work is here in the dry store and I have had it out on the bench the whole morning. It has done some four hundred hours by the log, which the makers would call a long life and I should call a reckless one. Here is what has gone wrong with it, in no order at all. The rubber of the collar is perished where the sun got at it, and I hold that a fortnight on a sunny quay does a dress more harm than a season in the sea. Two of the twelve corselet studs are drawn and their tapped holes stripped. The air pipe: the canvas outer covering chafed clean through at eleven feet from the helmet, which is where it takes the ladder rung. The rubber beneath was bulged but had not burst. It would have burst next week. The non-return valve at the helmet is gummed with verdigris and slow to seat. That is the one which kills a man, for if the pipe parts and that valve does not shut, the pressure below drives him up into his own helmet. The pump leathers are hard and the delivery is down by a third against the gauge. Condemn the pipe outright, I say, and the collar with it. Yours ever, A. L.

INSURANCE ASSESSMENT. Survey of the wreck, Gantock shoal, 1866. Measurement of burial. Method. A graduated rod, 6 feet, marked in inches, is set vertically against the frame and pressed down until it meets firm bottom. The reading taken at the mud surface is entered as the depth of burial. Each frame is measured on both sides and the mean recorded. Bottom: black peat mud, soft to about 14 inches, firmer beneath. Frame 3: exposed 2 ft 9 in above the mud; buried 1 ft 4 in. Frame 4: exposed 2 ft 1 in; buried 1 ft 11 in. Frame 5: exposed 11 in; buried 3 ft 2 in. Frame 6: not exposed. Rod met timber 3 in below the surface; buried depth not ascertainable with this rod. Remark. The measurements are to be repeated at the same six frames at every survey. Whether the exposed portion diminishes by silting or by wasting of the timber cannot be told from a single visit and requires the series. Assessor's initials appended.

Salvage claim, 1877. The Ardmore approaches. Schedule B: conditions attaching to the articles recovered. Articles lifted from below seawater, some part of them out of peat. Condition 1. Every article to be kept wet from the moment of lifting. Immersed, not merely covered over. Condition 2. No article to be laid out in the yard, nor on the quay, nor in any open place where sun or wind may reach it. This applies although the article appear hard and sound. Condition 3. Tanks to be topped up daily. Sacking over. Water renewed weekly. Reason, entered for the information of the yard. Seawater carries salts into the substance of an article throughout the years of its immersion. On drying, the water goes off and the salts crystallise within, and the growing crystals burst the article apart from the inside. Timber checks and splits; iron scales and flakes away; pottery and stone spall at the surface. The mischief is not reversible. Once dried, no after treatment restores the article. Claim is made upon the articles as delivered wet. Any loss arising from drying in the yard is not chargeable to the claimants.

CUSTOMS ENTRY. The Gantock shoal. 1874. Entry No. 402. Amended. Article: waterlogged oak, four pieces, and two fragments of porous stoneware, recovered from the shoal. Condition on landing: saturated, sound to the eye, no value declared. Condition at second inspection, nineteen days later: damaged. Entry amended accordingly. Cause, as stated by the surveyor: 1. Such material is porous throughout, and holds sea water in its pores. 2. On drying, the water goes off and the salt does not, but comes out of solution within the pores as crystals. 3. The salt so formed takes up more room than it did in solution, and works in the pores as a wedge works. 4. The surfaces are thereby lifted, powdered and shed. The stoneware has flaked away in scales; the oak has bloomed white and crumbles at every edge. 5. Damp weather and dry weather following upon one another aggravate the mischief, the salt taking up water and coming out again at each turn. Recommendation minuted: goods of this character to be soaked in fresh water, the water being changed until it is sweet, before ever they are laid in a dry store. Duty: nil. Entry closed.

LABORATORY NOTE. Dry store, Kilbrannan Sound, 1866. Half of what the boats bring in is no wreck at all, and the trick of the thing is to know it before you have paid a man to lift it. Nature does not saw. That is the whole of the matter. A drift log rolled down a burn and tumbled about in the sea comes to us rounded at every angle and worn smooth as a bone, its ends splintered or torn where the tree gave way, keeping its bark in patches and the swell of its own growth. Worked timber tells on itself at once. There is the flat face; the square corner that no wave ever cut; the saw kerf running true across the grain; and above all the fastenings, the bolt hole dead round and dead straight through six inches of oak, or the black iron stain about it where the bolt has rusted out and left its ghost behind. Rule for the shed: look first for a hole, second for a straight edge, third for the tool marks. Two of the three and it is ours. None of the three and it is firewood. So catalogued this day.

CARGO MANIFEST. Shipped in the Tarbert narrows, 1863. Bronze, in pigs, forty-two in number. Remarks by the shipper's man, written in the margin because there is nowhere else to put them. I would not sign for this parcel until I had it assayed, and I had two ounces drilled from each of six pigs and sent up for the figures. What comes back is a return of tin and of lead, and I set down here what I take them to mean, for the buyer's benefit. The tin is the making of the metal. The more of it, up to a point, the harder the casting, the closer the grain, and the longer and clearer the note when you strike it. That is why the bell-founders run their tin high and pay for it. The lead is another matter. A little of it makes the metal run sweetly into the mould and fill every corner, and the moulders are fond of it for that. But lead does not alloy true; it lies about in the metal, softens it, and kills the ring dead. Where I see lead above a few parts in the hundred I take it that somebody has been cheapening the mixture. This parcel returns tin sufficient and lead low. I have signed accordingly.

DIVE LOG. Sanda roads. 1875. Dive 7. Down 10h. 42m., up 11h. 19m. Depth 7 fathoms. Bottom peat. Slack water, no stream. Raised: one sand-cast bronze bracket, broken across the web. Examination on deck, the fracture being fresh and clean: Blowholes. Numerous, from a pin's head to 3/16 in. across, lying in a band about 1/2 in. below the upper face, that being the cope side of the mould. Gas trapped in the casting; the mould was vented badly. Cold shut. One, running 2 1/4 in. across the web at the thin section, showing as a seam with rounded lips and a skin upon either face. Two streams of metal met there and did not unite, the metal having been run too cold or too slow. Draw. A sink of about 1/16 in. over the boss where the section thickens, no feeder head having been set above it. Sand inclusions. Three, the largest 1/8 in., with the sand still in them. Remark. The web measures 5/8 in. where the drawing calls for 3/4 in. The fracture has run through the cold shut and the band of blowholes together. No load worth the name would have been wanted to part it. The casting was bad out of the mould, and the sea is not to be blamed for it.

Harbour Master's Log. Loch Ryan. 1870. Entry made at the request of the Trustees, who ask how the founder from the works satisfied himself as to the recovered metal without an assay. Method observed: 1. Piece suspended free upon a cord. Founder states it must hang clear, a hand upon it killing the note. 2. Struck once at the rim with a light hammer. 3. The note listened for, and its length counted out. Founder's rules, as given by him: Long clear ring, high in pitch, well sustained: much tin, hard metal, close grain. Bell-stuff. Short note, lower, dying at once: less tin, or lead present. Softer metal, open grain. Dead thud, no note at all: a flaw, a crack, or sand caught in the casting, whatever the alloy may be. He tried eleven pieces in this manner in under ten minutes and set four aside. The four were afterward assayed and found as he had said in three cases out of the four. Metal held in dry store pending sale. Entered by the Harbour Master.

REPORT OF SURVEY. Sanda roads, 1873. Upon the pattern shop and moulding floor of the works, made at the instance of the proprietors. Upon the patterns. It is found that the same are wrought in well seasoned yellow pine, and that the patternmaker sets out his work by the contraction rule proper to the metal, so that the casting when cold shall come to the dimension required. Further, that draught is given upon every vertical face, that the work may be drawn from the sand without tearing; that all inward angles are filleted; and that the surfaces are painted and blacked to leave the sand clean. Upon the sand. It is found that the moulding sand is a loam of sufficient bond, tempered with water and riddled fine upon the face of the pattern, backed with coarser sand from the floor, and rammed by degrees, neither so slack that the mould shall wash nor so hard that the gases cannot escape. Upon the mould. It is found that the box is parted and the pattern drawn without injury; that the mould is vented freely with the wire; that runner, riser and ingates are properly cut; and that the whole is dried before pouring. The practice of the shop is found workmanlike, and no exception is taken.

Salvage Claim. Kilbrannan Sound. 1865. I am George Nairn, of Campbeltown, and I make this claim for metal lifted out of the peat in the Sound this summer. I will say plain what it is worth, for I sell such stuff every month of my life. What I have raised: copper sheathing, 3 cwt; mixed brass and gunmetal fittings, 11 cwt; lead, 6 cwt; iron, the best part of two ton. What the market gives for it. Copper is the money. The Liverpool breakers were paying 8d. the pound for clean sheathing last month, and 6d. for it foul with nails and concretion, and they weigh it foul at that. Brass and gunmetal, 5d. to 7d., according as it is dressed and sorted. Lead, 18s. the hundredweight, and no trouble to sell. Iron out of the sea is hardly worth its freight, 30s. the ton if a man is lucky, the buyers saying it is wasted through and through, and they are not far wrong. So the money is all in the yellow metal, and that is why men will dive a whole season on a wreck for her fastenings and let her frames lie where they are. I claim upon the above at the customary third. - G. Nairn, his hand.

Book of the Works, 1877. Memorandum entered in the ledger, there being no other book kept in this office fit to hold it. The partners having resolved that the loss reports accumulated these thirty years shall no longer lie in the presses of the counting house in the disorder in which they have hitherto lain, I have undertaken their arrangement, and set down here the method, that whoever comes after me may follow it. Every report, be it a master's letter, an underwriter's survey, a newspaper cutting, or a diver's statement, is given a number in one continuous series; and that number is written in ink upon the paper itself and never upon the wrapper, wrappers being a thing that go astray. The number, the date, the vessel if she be named, the place of loss, and the name of the sender are then entered in this book, in that order and in no other. Papers are stored flat, in the dry press by the chimney and not in the low press by the yard door, out of which two bundles came this spring soaked and mouldered, no better than the waterlogged oak the divers land from the Ardmore approaches. Nothing is to be lent out of this office. Copies may be made. Entered by the clerk of the works.
